articles.title: Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen
articles.summary:
Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land

Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen,…

blocks.text: Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen, approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.

The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador to Yemen, Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.

Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west.

blocks.caption: A Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter is seen purportedly firing at a Houthi position near Dhubab in Taiz. Photograph: Southern Giants Brigades/Reuters

blocks.text: Houthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded.

The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that the Houthis have stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”.
There has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims about Yemeni government advances issued at the beginning of the week.

Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people.

The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel.

Southern Giant forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. Their forces are now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait.

articles.title: EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ request
articles.summary:
Lithuania and Canada were also pressured to withdraw, and days before #Disinfo2026, logos were wiped off website

The Trump…
articles.byline: Aisha Down in London, Joseph Gedeon in Washington and Jennifer Rankin in Brussels

blocks.text: The Trump administration pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship of a leading European conference on disinformation, with Canada, Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service subsequently agreeing to do so, the Guardian understands.

The conference, #Disinfo2026, taking place Wednesday and Thursday, is the annual meetup of Europe’s counter-disinformation community and has drawn hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania. It is run by an independent Brussels non-profit, EU Disinfo Lab.

Days before the conference, the logos of its main supporters – the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry – were wiped off its website.

Photos of the event shared with the Guardian also show white stickers affixed over the logos of these organisations printed on official conference materials, appearing to indicate they were struck from the program in haste.

blocks.caption: A #Disinfo2026 flyer shows portions blocked out. Photograph: Obtained by The Guardian

blocks.text: Three persons familiar with the matter, including European officials, confirmed that the US state department had been in touch with multiple governments over their support for the conference.

Internal state department documents seen by the Guardian also show US officials thanking Lithuania for “taking US concerns seriously”. The document says Washington was “grateful” Lithuania supposedly found a panel framing the US as a foreign information threat “reprehensible and surprising” and welcomed its decision to limit involvement in the conference.

That panel – called “USA as a FIMI threat: adapt, acknowledge, push back”, with the acronym FIMI referring to “foreign information manipulation and interference” – took place Wednesday. It explored how Europe’s disinformation community could rebuild resilience without Washington, and is the first time the conference appears to have entertained the idea that the US could be a disinformation actor in Europe. Sources and the internal document indicate the state department was explicitly focused on this panel, which included three American speakers, among them a former CIA officer.
According to one person familiar with the deliberations, other communications appeared to originate from the office of Sarah B Rogers, the US undersecretary of state for public diplomacy.

Nina Jankowicz, a former US official and disinformation expert who in 2022 briefly headed the Biden administration’s Disinformation Governance Board, which Republicans assailed as a vehicle for policing Americans’ speech, said she understood that Washington had pressured Lithuania and Canada to withdraw from the conference. The Guardian understood from French officials that France was contacted as well.

“What this amounts to is a purported defender of free speech at the state department using the enormous power of the US government to try to pressure Americans from criticizing their government,” said Jankowicz.

In statements, Lithuania, Canada and the EU said the program of the conference did not align with their official views on the US role in disinformation – although that program had been in place for months before they withdrew their support, since June.

“Lithuania has cancelled its participation in ‘Disinfo 2026’ as several parts of the conference programme differ from the official position of the Government,” Lithuania’s foreign ministry wrote in a statement.

Global Affairs Canada “carefully assesses participation in, and sponsorship of, external events on a case-by-case basis,” GAC spokesperson Samantha Lafleur said. “Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference.”
Canadian officials are still participating in the conference, Lafleur added.

An EU spokesperson confirmed that the European External Action Service had decided to withdraw its support from the conference because “the organisers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU.”
EU officials, the Guardian understands, did not agree with the characterisation of the US as a disinformation actor.
Despite withdrawing its branding as an official supporter, the EU continues to fund the conference.

In its latest report on foreign information manipulation and interference threats, published in March, the EU’s diplomatic service named Russia and China as “threat actors” without any negative reference to the US.
A diplomatic source at France’s foreign ministry said “there’s absolutely no reason for us to change our commitments” when it came to supporting the conference.

“We stick to supporting civil society. It’s not just principled, it’s operational,” she said, adding that the conference was a “laboratory” that helped Europe develop key policy around disinformation.

The US state department has taken an increasingly interventionist posture towards free speech and civil society in Europe over the past year. The Guardian has revealed that the state department is awarding millions of dollars in non-competitive grants to organisations across the continent supportive of Trump’s agenda.

Lithuania’s withdrawal comes just after the prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevicius, said Lithuania would pay for a permanent US military base if the US agreed, a day after Trump said he would consider the request. Sinkevicius called a lasting American presence a critical guarantee of deterrence against Russia.
“They are great people, so we will certainly look at it,” the US president said on Monday.

Sinkevicius said he first proposed the idea in a meeting with Trump’s envoy John Coale, and called it a “critically important guarantee of deterrence and security.” Lithuania, a member of the EU and Nato, borders Russia and its close ally Belarus.
The US has kept a rotating armoured battalion of almost 1,000 troops in the country since 2019, the US Army has noted.

articles.title: Hegseth tells USS Lincoln sailors controversial deployment ‘wasn’t easy’
articles.summary:
Pentagon chief tries to play down problems onboard carrier as it returns to dock after 260 days at sea without port call

Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, told service members on the…

blocks.text: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, told service members on the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday that their deployment “wasn’t easy” as the carrier prepares to dock after spending over 260 consecutive days at sea without a port call, setting a navy record.

For months, there have been widespread concerns since reports first emerged of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health onboard. In his remarks on Wednesday, however, Hegseth again sought to play down the issues.

Instead, he condemned “a few folks in the media” who he accused of trying to “turn” the Lincoln’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.

“I never say this lightly, but I’m the one who signed that orders go twice to extend you,” Hegseth, who has pledged to restore the “warrior ethos” to the US military, told the service members on Wednesday. “I plead guilty.”

Hegseth announced that those onboard the vessel, which is set to arrive in San Diego later this week, would be awarded the presidential unit citation, which, according to the US military is conferred on units of the armed forces “for extraordinary heroism in action against an armed enemy”.

The USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group “did what no other carrier strike group has ever done”, he declared on Wednesday. “We asked you to do more, and you know what you did? You did more. And it wasn’t easy, and there wasn’t easy resupply.”

The US carrier, with roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard, left San Diego in November 2025, initially bound for the Pacific and expected to return in the spring. But after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, the Lincoln was redirected to the Middle East, to support US operations in the region.

Its deployment was extended, and the carrier spent over 250 consecutive days at sea without a port visit, setting a navy record, as the war disrupted regional resupply routes and traditional hubs. The deployment was described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era” by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command.

As Donald Trump struggled to end the war with Iran, and the Lincoln’s deployment dragged on, reports emerged over the summer of shortages of food and basic supplies, and deteriorating mental health and morale among some crew members, including that two crew members had attempted to jump overboard.

At the time, senior Trump administration officials dismissed the reports. Hegseth claimed they “completely misrepresented” the reality, while Trump, when asked in August whether the deployment had gone on too long, responded, “Not nearly long enough” – a remark that upset some naval families.

The reports about the conditions on the Lincoln caused concern among some military health experts, veterans and families of sailors onboard, and drew outrage from Democratic lawmakers, including several who demanded more information from the Pentagon.
The Lincoln was relieved from its deployment later in August, as the USS George Washington aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East to take its place.

But in recent weeks, as the Lincoln has headed back to San Diego, a new disclosure about the carrier has renewed scrutiny. Acting navy secretary Hung Cao acknowledged last month that eight service members from the Lincoln and its strike group had attempted suicide during the deployment. He was responding to questions from Kirsten Gillibrand, the the Democratic senator.

As Hegseth delivered his remarks on the Lincoln, Gillibrand criticized him, stating that “our service members deserve better than a photo-op. They deserve real accountability for this administration’s failures”.

Other Democratic lawmakers have requested that navy leaders provide an accounting of the eight suicide attempts, and have also asked navy leaders to detail the steps they will take to “protect sailors’ mental health and wellbeing during future extended deployments”.

As the Lincoln returns home this week, another aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, was recently dispatched to the Middle East. Navy officials have said they are taking steps to prevent similar problems during future deployments, including loading up the vessel with additional supplies, and improving communication with families.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Isaias near Mexico is forecast to become a hurricane
articles.summary:
Isaias, which succeeded Tropical Depression Nine, would be the first hurricane of the belated Atlantic season

Tropical Storm Isaias formed early on Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern…

blocks.text: Tropical Storm Isaias formed early on Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters said it was expected to strengthen into the first hurricane of the belated Atlantic season, as early as Thursday, before hitting the US Gulf coast later in the week.

Isaias succeeded Tropical Depression Nine as it strengthened overnight. It was located about 285 miles (460km) west of Progreso, Mexico, and about 580 miles south-west of where the Mississippi River spills into the Gulf of Mexico in Louisiana, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC). The storm on Wednesday morning had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65km/h) and was moving east to north-east at 8mph.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905.
Communities in the potential path of Isaias moved quickly to prepare for landfall, forecast as soon as Friday evening.

Some Gulf oil wells paused production and an Alabama beach city canceled a weekend festival known to draw thousands of tourists. Florida’s governor declared a state of emergency for more than one-third of the state’s counties.
Isaias could become a major category 3 hurricane, with winds of 111mph (178 km/h) or stronger, before it strikes land, said Michael Brennan, director of the NHC.
“We’re expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast beginning Friday and continuing into the weekend,” Brennan said in a video briefing Wednesday.

It was not immediately known where the storm may make landfall on the US Gulf coast. The NHC issued a hurricane watch from Bay St Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida. The watch means hurricane conditions are possible within 48 hours.

The hurricane center’s initial projections said the center of Isaias could come onshore somewhere between eastern Louisiana and the western Florida Panhandle. People in those areas were urged to prepare for the storm.

“There is an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast,” the hurricane center, based in Miami, Florida, said. “Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place.”

Forecasters added that there was “uncertainty in where the system makes the northeast turn and how fast it moves toward the coast”. The direction of the storm could see it make landfall where Alabama meets Florida early on Saturday, but the NHC reiterated that the exact path was uncertain.

In Gulf Shores, Alabama, the storm threat caused organizers to cancel the National Shrimp Festival that had been scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year.

The storm comes as the Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year owing to a particularly strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity in the Pacific has been above average.

This year’s huge El Niño is causing climate chaos around the world. Temperate records have already been broken, with extreme heat reported from western Europe to California. Meanwhile, Bangkok is suffering massive flooding and the weather phenomenon is projected to cause a further 450,000 deaths globally by February.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: NASA's Curiosity rover takes striking image of dawn on Mars
articles.summary: NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing ‌jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues…

image.caption: A view of the Martian surface taken by NASA's Curiosity rover on Aug. 11. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/Reuters)

blocks.text: Science·New

NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing ‌jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth's planetary neighbour.
Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator
Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a five-kilometre-tall mountain rising from the crater floor.
The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover's Mastcam camera about ​an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved ​cliffs in the distance.

"The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far," said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist.

NASA believes that some kind of wind-blown sediment landed in the crater from nearby volcanic activity. Once it hardened into rock, "eons of wind carved ‌up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs," Vasvada said.

The yardang layer most likely formed about three billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 16 ⁠kilometres across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp.
But the layers appears to have been added on later, he said.
"It's above what geologists call an ‌unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top."
Rover making gradual ascent up mountain
The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of nearly a kilometre in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars, according to NASA.

Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a ​period of the planet's geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have learned more about bodies of water — lakes and streams — that long ago covered this region, at ⁠a time when Mars was wetter and warmer than the cold and desolate place it is today.

Mars rover snaps pictures of giant, dark sand dunes

blocks.text: Vasavada said NASA hopes ⁠Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at which time it will use its instruments to ⁠scrutinize ⁠the geology there.

Curiosity has been studying the ​geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harboring microbial life. It is one of two ​NASA rovers operating on Mars. The ⁠Perseverance rover is currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere.
Curiosity's new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly.
"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky," Vasavada said.
"But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades ⁠of blue. It's like Earth, but ‌it's definitely Mars."

articles.title: Judge orders officials to preserve all evidence tied to Christa Pike’s botched execution
articles.summary:
Judge tells Tennessee officials all items in execution room must be saved as Pike remains restrained in hospital bed

A judge ordered Tennessee officials on Wednesday to preserve all…

blocks.text: A judge ordered Tennessee officials on Wednesday to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution attempt on convicted murderer Christa Pike, as it emerged that the state has refused pleas from medical staff to allow her to be unshackled from her hospital bed.

At a hearing in Nashville on Wednesday, judge I’Ashea Myles said: “Anything that was in the actual room” during the attempted execution a week ago must be preserved by the state, including all drugs, intravenous lines and tubing used in the death chamber.
The order came as Pike’s lawyers said she has pneumonia, a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms, after she regained consciousness on Tuesday.
“The first thing she said was: ‘Where am I and who are you?’,” one of Pike’s lawyers said on Wednesday afternoon.

Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber last Wednesday after two supposedly lethal doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital. She had been on a ventilator, with an unknown prognosis, before she woke and spoke on Tuesday.

“There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people. She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family … I think she is angry and confused about everything right now,” one of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, said.

The updates came after a contentious court hearing where Pike’s legal team accused Tennessee officials of “secreting away” evidence. Attorney Luke Ihnen said items from the attempted execution could be key to future legal challenges by Pike, should the state attempt to kill her again.

“The state has made no promises that Ms Pike will not be subject to a future execution, and the evidence that we are seeking to preserve now is relevant for any future challenge that she makes, because as we pled in January, the same thing is likely to happen,” Ihnen said.

Pike survived a lengthy procedure and the large doses of the sedative as Tennessee officials had attempted to put her to death, in a case that shocked many in the US and created headlines around the world.

At a press conference after Wednesday’s hearing, Spivey said it was unclear “what if any function” Pike would regain in her arms. “Her hands look like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” Spivey said.
Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm.

“Based on our understanding, medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request [by the Tennessee correction department],” he told Myles earlier. He added: “We would also amend our request and ask for that relief.”

Witnesses to the attempted execution of Pike described how they heard her breathing raggedly after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her and was declared to be in critical condition.
after newsletter promotion

After the botched execution attempt, Spivey called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.

Her lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.

There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or a lot of the drug missed her vein and went into tissue, that one of her veins, which were problematic and this fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, or that the drug was faulty, or a combination.
Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her.

Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years.

articles.title: Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades
articles.summary:
Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms

Two men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have…

blocks.text: Two men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less.

A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward.

Ward, who was freed in 2017 after serving 10 years more than his one-year minimum and was later recalled to prison, was also in court, sitting in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced.
Relatives of Ings and Bennett hugged in the public gallery at Wolverhampton crown court on Wednesday as Mr Justice Choudhury told them the IPPs had been “cancelled”.
Choudhury said Bennett would instead be sentenced to four years and 264 days, Ward to two years, and Ings to 42 months with a 30-month extended licence.
All three men’s original sentences were quashed and replaced after they argued that judges had wrongly found them to be dangerous or had not considered alternative sentences.

Choudhury, sitting with the magistrate Norma Grant, told the appellants: “You have already spent considerably longer than those [replacement] sentences in custody. The effect is that you, Mr Bennett, and you, Mr Ings, will be entitled to release without further supervision, and you, Mr Ward, will no longer be subject to supervision.”

The ruling came after the CCRC referred the cases of the three men back to the crown court to review minimum terms imposed on them by judges in Wolverhampton, Reading and Leicester respectively in 2006 and 2007.

Bennett and Ings, now both 38, were 17 when they committed offences that led to them being classed as dangerous offenders and given indeterminate sentences with respective minimum terms of 24 months and 21 months in 2007 and 2006.

Bennett was originally sentenced at Wolverhampton crown court in May 2007 after being found guilty of reckless arson for setting fire to items in the loft space of an empty council property, and admitting criminal damage and burglary.

Ings was sentenced to detention for public protection after appearing at East Berkshire youth court in March 2006 and admitting offences including a robbery in an underpass and an assault on a teenager in a fast food outlet.

Ward, now 41, was 21 when he was given a one-year minimum sentence in 2006 at Leicester crown court for arson and criminal damage. He admitted arson – after setting fire to items in his prison cell while serving time for assault – and was released in 2017, but was later recalled to prison and remained in custody until August this year.

Muin Boase, representing Bennett, successfully argued that the judge who sentenced him in 2007 did not give proper weight to his youth, lack of maturity and capacity to change after a difficult childhood.
In its ruling, the appeal court said there had been no proper basis for the original finding of dangerousness.

Detention for public protection and imprisonment for public protection (DPP and IPP) sentences were abolished in 2012, having been made available to tackle offenders considered a significant risk to the public in 2005.

The law was changed to stop courts handing out IPP sentences after warnings that they were being applied too widely, but the abolition was not retrospective, meaning many prisoners serving such sentences are still behind bars.
The government has faced calls to take action on IPP jail terms, with the former justice secretary Ken Clarke saying last month that ministers should not to be too cautious.

His comments came a week after the current justice secretary, Alex Norris, told MPs that the government planned to bring forward legislation to end IPP sentences “once and for all” by the end of this parliament.
More than 2,000 prisoners remain held indefinitely under IPP sentences, with 99% past their original tariff and 80% having served 10 years or more.
Additional reporting by the Press Association

articles.title: WHO wants more answers from Russia about lab worker's death, as pneumonic plague concerns linger
articles.summary: A top official with the World Health Organization said Wednesday the UN health agency doesn't know how a lab worker in Siberia died amid concerns about plague, and is urging Russia to provide more…

image.caption: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, where a lab technician worked before her death on Oct. 2 from pneumonia. The World Health Organization is urging Russia to be more forthcoming with information about the case, as authorities insist her illness was not related to

blocks.text: Health·New

A top official with the World Health Organization said Wednesday the UN health agency doesn't know how a lab worker in Siberia died amid concerns about plague, and is urging Russia to provide more information.
UN health agency also checking unconfirmed reports of 2nd case linked to lab
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Oct 07, 2026 3:14 PM EDT | Last Updated: 15 minutes ago
A top official with the UN's health agency doesn't know how a lab worker in Siberia died amid concerns about plague, and she's urging Russia to provide more information.

There have been questions and concerns about the death of the 28-year-old woman, identified in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, amid speculation she died of pneumonic plague and that her death may be connected pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.

Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management at the World Health Agency (WHO), said the agency doesn't know the cause of the woman's Oct. 2 death, and "this is why we need more information."
"We don't understand how she was infected," Van Kerkhove said during a news briefing in Geneva.
The WHO is also seeking more information about unconfirmed media reports of a second case of pneumonia of "undetermined cause" connected to the Irkutsk lab, in southeastern Siberia.
WHO director general Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the agency could not verify the credibility of the reports but is seeking clarification from the relevant officials in Russia.

In a tersely worded statement, Russia's official public health and consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, does not link the first case to pneumonic plague, saying only that "extensive" testing found no evidence the lab worker's illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with.

items: Did a Russian lab worker die from pneumonic plague? What we know — and don't know

blocks.text: Russia has said she died of pneumonia — a "typical" acute respiratory viral infection — and its health authorities have found no cases of plague recently, the WHO has said, acknowledging that pneumonia is commonplace and that cases of COVID-19 and rhinovirus were present among the some 200 people monitored since that death.
Pneumonic plague is a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.

Plague is an infectious disease caused by a bacterium known as Yersinia pestis, or Y. pestis, that is carried by small mammals and generally spread by the fleas that feed off them. It can be treated with antibiotics but can be deadly if left untreated.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, which was recently confirmed as the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak of the disease.
What we know about the suspected plague death in Russia
Russia insists no plague cases
Moscow previously informed the WHO that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region.
Russian health authorities reported a full range of preventive measures had been carried out —including tracing the dead woman's contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests, the WHO said.
The Russian note relayed to The Associated Press by the WHO said the test showed "no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts."
The organization said it has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of the second case.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov referred all questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which does not mention suspected plague in its reports.
In its latest statement Tuesday, the agency said "the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region … is calm."
Authorities were completing a "complex of prophylactic measures and medical observation over contacts," it said, adding that so far they have found two cases of COVID-19 and two of rhinovirus.
Mother not notified

The news outlet Lyudi Baikala identified Shipilova as the deceased lab worker and said she first was hospitalized with cold symptoms Sept. 29, in the nearby town of Shelekhov, and died three days later.
It quoted colleagues as saying she was a highly qualified and diligent researcher, and emphasized that security rules at the facility are extremely strict.
The report quoted Shipilova's neighbours as saying a team of disinfection experts did several cleanups of her apartment, leaving a strong antiseptic smell.
Researchers work in the institute's lab in this undated photo released in 2019. (Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/Handout/The Associated Press)

Shipilova's mother, who worked as a doctor in the past, described her daughter as hard-working and dedicated, according to independent Russian news outlet Glubina, adding that she had not received official documents describing the cause of death.
Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said she died of a "particularly dangerous infection" and everyone who came into contact with her has remained under medical supervision.
The hospital where she died was placed under quarantine, no longer admitting or discharging patients, although its outpatient clinic has continued operating, according to Mayor Maxim Modin.
WHO urges transparency
Russian authorities have, however kept a tight lid on information and the speculation she died of pneumonic plague.

While the case has grabbed international attention, Russian state TV and other national state-controlled media have steered clear of the subject. Some state-sponsored news outlets withdrew earlier reports about the case.

items: Russian officials say no cases of plague in city where lab technician died
At 'crucial' moment for pandemic preparedness, experts say world isn't ready

blocks.text: Vasily Vlassov, professor at the department of health-care administration and economics at Russia's Higher School of Economics, says it's not clear whether more transparency was possible if those dealing with the situation didn't have enough certainty, and "maybe, they still don't."
Deceiving the public "always turns out to be harmful," he said, and distrust of Russia's official narrative is "natural" and "almost inevitable."

Judy Twigg, professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, notes that Russia criminalized "false information" about threats to public safety in 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic, "so silence is the one safe move for everyone below the top."
"Personalist regimes without electoral accountability tend to treat bad news as a loyalty problem rather than focusing on the actual problem to be addressed," she said.

articles.title: Canada to extend assisted dying exclusion for people whose sole condition is mental illness
articles.summary:
Legislation an effort by ruling Liberals to address growing clash over who has access to doctor-assisted death

Canada’s federal government said Wednesday it would advance legislation to…

blocks.text: Canada’s federal government said Wednesday it would advance legislation to prevent people whose sole health condition is mental illness from accessing euthanasia, an effort by the ruling Liberal party to address a clash in the country over who has access to physician-assisted death.

Under the current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessing medical assistance in dying (Maid) to end their lives. But that ban – due to be lifted in March – has divided lawmakers over whether to permit this expansion of the Maid program.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the justice minister, Sean Fraser, said his government would indefinitely bar people whose sole condition is mental illness from accessing the program. He said that while there was no “perfect consensus” on this issue, upcoming legislation reflected the “correct” approach.

Earlier this year, a government committee concluded the government should expand access to Maid and should “indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness from eligibility for medical assistance in dying”. That report also flagged the need for “increased and more equitable access” to mental health services.

Canada’s medical assistance in dying (Maid) laws, drawn up after a 2015 supreme court decision, initially only permitted those who are terminally ill to be eligible for the procedure. But in 2019, a Quebec judge ruled that restricting access to those who had a “reasonably foreseeable death” was unconstitutional, forcing federal lawmakers to amend and expand the existing laws.

In 2021, the law was updated so adults could receive an assisted death if two doctors confirmed an irremediable physical condition causing immense suffering that cannot be relieved. Given the uncertainty surrounding mental illness, lawmakers in 2021 initially put a temporary exclusion in place for people who suffer solely from a mental illness. They renewed that pause in 2023 and 2024.

According to the latest government figures, the vast majority of Maid deaths – 95.6% – involved people whose natural death was considered “reasonably foreseeable”. Only 4.4% were cases in which death was not considered reasonably foreseeable. Those include people with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and incurable neurological disease that can causes profound disability and immense suffering.

The Liberal party’s legislation is also an effort to ward off a private member’s bill that would amend the section of the criminal code covering Maid so that “a mental disorder is not a grievous and irremediable medical condition”.

Advocates for expanding Maid to include mental illness alone say the current rules violate their constitutional rights and access to healthcare. Fraser acknowledged to reporters that a federal case, led by the advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada, to challenge the government’s previous decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness, could affect the upcoming bill.

Fraser said lawmakers would also work to decriminalize what are known as advanced requests, effectively giving people suffering from some illnesses such as Alzheimer’s the chance to choose Maid before their illness deprives them of the capacity to consent.

At present, Quebec is the only jurisdiction that permits the use of these requests. Fraser gave no specifics on the timing of the legislation but said that provinces will decide whether to provide advance requests. While the province of Alberta has already said it will not permit advance requests, the jusice minister said the bill attempts to ensure “the doctors who provide the services will not be treated as criminals for doing so”.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields under fire as 2 vendors say they're still owed money
articles.summary: Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival won praise for its all-woman lineup and charitable focus on reproductive rights and fighting gender-based violence. But the festival is coming under fire…

image.caption: Olivia Rodrigo performs at the Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival in Irvine, Calif., on Aug. 29, 2026. Two vendors at the festival are criticizing it for poor working conditions and for not being fully paid for their services. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival won praise for its all-woman lineup and charitable focus on reproductive rights and fighting gender-based violence. But the festival is coming under fire from two vendors alleging they endured poor working conditions and haven’t received proper payment for their services.
Vendors also allege poor working conditions at Aug. 29 concert
Olivia Rodrigo’s inaugural festival, Daisy Chain Fields, won praise for its all-woman lineup and charitable focus on reproductive rights and fighting gender-based violence.
But the festival is coming under fire from two vendors who allege they endured poor working conditions and haven’t received proper payment for their services.
The one-day festival brought swarms of fans to Great Park in Irvine, Calif., to hear performances by Chappell Roan, Doechii, Mitski, Bikini Kill and Rodrigo herself.

All performers donated their time, with proceeds from the festival going to 10 organizations centering women's rights, including Planned Parenthood, National Women's Law Center, Black Mamas Matter and the National Institute for Reproductive Health.
The $10 million US initially raised by the festival was then matched by Melinda French Gates to bring the total to $20 million.
But more than a month after the festival took place, two vendors are sharing that the festival experience was far from perfect for them.

Mary Chacon, owner of Ugly Oats Kitchen, posted "An Open Letter to Olivia Rodrigo," on Instagram on Tuesday, alleging she still hasn’t "been paid out of our sales (in violation of our contract)" yet, which prompted her to share her experience vending at Daisy Chain Fields.

Chacon stated that the subcontractor in charge of food vendors, DLS Events, only provided piecemeal information on setup and didn’t tell them about a free staff food area, which she said was also so far away from their booth that they couldn’t access it.
Rodrigo performs at Daisy Chain Fields on Aug. 29. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

After she was told by DLS Events that the festival would fine them if they ran out of food, she said she baked thousands of cookies — only to see very few sales, which she attributes to organizers’ poor planning.

"Ugly Oats is a micro bakery run out of my apartment. I, as a mom investing my own money, have no extra funds," Chacon wrote, adding that she will be "forever grateful for the opportunity to be present at a historic feminist event," and that she hopes issues will be resolved for vendors next year.

CBC News has reached out for comment from Rodrigo’s team, as well as C3 Presents, the company that produced the event, and the two companies highlighted by Chacon as managing vendors for the festival: DLS Events and Jetty Event Productions.
'Vendors are talent, too'

Shortly after Ugly Oats Kitchen posted on Tuesday, custom fortune cookie company Por Suerte shared in their own post that they had a similar experience at Daisy Chain Fields, thanking Ugly Oats Kitchen "for starting the conversation."

The business, which is operated solely by owner Veronica Licha Lopez, posted on Instagram that there was poor communication from organizers in the weeks leading up to the event, and that her business experienced a "significant financial loss" by participating.

items: Olivia Rodrigo makes history with Daisy Chain Fields and wears a piece of Vancouver in the process
Olivia Rodrigo's music festival raises $20M US for charities that help women and girls

blocks.text: "We’re still waiting to be paid. After everything we spent to participate, we have still not received what we are owed for the event," the post stated.
"Supporting women shouldn’t stop at putting women on a stage … Because vendors are talent, too."
Rodrigo hasn’t publicly commented on the criticisms.

Although charity music festivals aren't a new concept — from 1985’s Live Aid concert to a virtual festival curated by Lady Gaga to raise money for COVID-19 relief in 2020 — Daisy Chain Fields is the first one to focus on women's and reproductive rights.

The festival sparked some concerns from local authorities in its immediate wake due to a heat wave bringing high temperatures during the event, and a traffic crush from the tens of thousands of fans. But city leaders told local media they are already on board to host the event next year.
Signs are displayed behind festivalgoers on the Marigold Stage at the Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

Rodrigo has been outspoken in the fight for reproductive rights, lambasting abortion bans ahead of the Daisy Chain Fields festival as not "pro-life" but "pro-control." During her GUTS tour in 2024/2025, she partnered with local women-focused charities and donated a portion of her ticket sales. She is currently on the North American leg of her Unraveled tour.

In the wake of the festival, Rodrigo shared on social media that it was "the greatest joy of my career," saying the event felt like "a collective hope that things can get better and a reminder of how much we really care about people at the end of the day."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan
articles.summary:
Party hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speech

Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish…

blocks.text: Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.
The Tory leader also said couples would be able to leave an additional tax-free sum of £1m to their families, as the party attempts to shore up its traditional base in southern England.

The move would mean the number of families paying inheritance tax – currently less than 5% do so – would fall by more than a half, Badenoch said, with the £6bn cost to be paid for by cuts the party says it has identified, including to the welfare bill.

“My ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it,” she told the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. “I believe the people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort. So this is my guarantee: no stamp duty when you buy your home, no mansion tax when you live in your home, and no inheritance tax on your home when you pass it to your children or grandchildren.”

The Tories’ policy plans announced this week – also including support with childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and repealing the mansion tax – have been firmly focused on affluent middle-class voters, many of whom deserted the party at the last election.

They have been welcomed by Conservative MPs and activists, who are relieved that Badenoch appears to be trying to shore up the party’s core support despite her natural proclivity to lean into culture wars on the right.

However, the inheritance tax plans are likely to raise fears about overheating the housing market, giving elderly homeowners an incentive to stay in large family homes rather than downsize. The move also prompted accusations the party was favouring the rich over struggling families.

In a statement, Tax Justice UK said: “Kemi Badenoch has just announced a massive inheritance tax giveaway to some of the wealthiest people in Britain. This is a reckless policy that will deprive public services of cash when they most need them.”

Stuart Adam, a senior economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes. These will mostly be people living in London and the south-east.”

Reform UK suggested Badenoch’s inheritance tax plans would affect only 2% of houses, the majority in London. Its finance spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said: “The Tory party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country.”

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair and minister for equalities, said: “The Tories haven’t changed. Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories’ choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead.”

blocks.caption: Badenoch acknowledged that the party faced a long road to recovery after its defeat at the 2024 general election.  Photograph: WPA/Getty

blocks.text: Despite the Tories appearing more united this week than they have done for years, Badenoch did acknowledge in her speech that the party, still polling lower than at the time of its catastrophic 2024 election defeat, faced a long path to recovery.

She issued an appeal to Reform voters to back her. “We let them down and we want them to come back home. They deserve better than Reform politicians,” she said. “We have changed our party. There is still a lot of work to do. People are looking through the shop window. They like what they see, but let’s be honest, not enough of them are buying it. We need to fix that.”

Senior Tories have been urging Badenoch to focus more on the economy, which they hope will help them to win back middle-class swing voters in their traditional heartlands, and to pivot away from culture wars and migration.

Badenoch added that economic growth would be the “central organising principle” of the next Conservative government, cutting red tape in areas such as planning, building a third runway at Heathrow and implementing a new energy policy, while also creating jobs.
after newsletter promotion
Most of her speech, however, was devoted to attacks on her opponents, with the Tories desperate to edge ahead of Reform in the polls and be seen once again as the main opposition party on the right.

Badenoch rejected calls from within her own party to “unite the right” by striking a deal with Nigel Farage’s party – reflecting warnings from her closest allies that doing so would risk toxifying the Conservative brand irrevocably.
She said: “A year ago, those politicians were measuring up the curtains for No 10. Now, some of them are measuring up the curtains for their prison cells.

“The circus goes on and on, and it will never stop because this is who Reform politicians are. So, to those who say ‘unite the right’, we are not uniting with that. People deserve better and we are going to give them better than that: character, conduct and standards matter.”

Badenoch also drew a sharp dividing line with Reform on race, after Suella Braverman, the former Conservative home secretary who defected to Farage’s party, suggested that minority ethnic people could not be English.

“I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English,” she said. “I remember back in the day when Ian Wright and John Barnes were playing. Nobody was questioning whether they were English. We certainly didn’t have sitting MPs questioning whether they were English.
“We must not let these people take us backwards. That is not the country we are. Reform MPs are openly questioning people’s identity.
“I don’t know whether you’ve noticed, but I am black. I am British. I am proud of my country. I’m proud of our history, all that we have done, and all that we will do in the world.”

Badenoch acknowledged that last year her leadership of the party had been under intense pressure. But she added: “Let me tell you, I’m not someone who gets written off, and neither is the Conservative party. There is a reason our party is still here after 200 years. We have adapted to every single challenge and every single age, and we are doing it again.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 35: No hand in joint bank accounts, payout
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte distanced her from the activities recorded under her BPI joint account with her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, involving purchased and unused…

blocks.text: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte distanced her from the activities recorded under her BPI joint account with her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, involving purchased and unused manager’s checks and a payout to alleged drug lord Sammy Uy.

Defense counsel Michael Poa made the argument after Marwin Galvez, BPI Central Metro Manila division head, testified that the joint account of the Vice President and her father purchased two sets of unutilized manager’s checks valued at P41 million and P55 million, respectively.
It was also revealed that P16 million of the amount was paid to Uy, who has been tagged by former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV as a drug personality.

“Nung lumabas ang mga accounts, tinitingnan namin itong mga accounts na ito and I was asked by the Vice President to verify kasi hindi niya natatandaan na may ganitong account at wala daw siyang transaksyon,” Poa said.
(When these came up, the Vice President asked me to verify because she does not recall these.)
“Wala siyang naging participation," Poa added.
(She has no participation in this.)
Manager's check: Ticket to concealment?

BPI’s Galvez also told the court that the owner of the manager’s check has an option not to use it and later deposit it again in his or her bank account within six months of the issuance of the manager’s check.
Upon the senator-judges’ inquiry, Galvez also confirmed that the amount indicated in the manager’s check won’t be reflected in the ending balance of the account holder at the end of the year.
This ‘floating’ scheme stirred the interest of the senator-judges.
Senator Bam Aquino said he was surprised that the scheme was allowed, while Senator Panfilo Lacson said the prosecution was clearly seeking to prove concealment on the part of the Vice President.
Lacson later added, although in jest, that Senator Lito Lapid is already contemplating buying a manager’s check worth P100 million.

Senator Vicente “Tito” Sotto III, for his part, said such a scheme is akin to the Filipino folk dance Tinikling wherein the dancers try to avoid being caught by striking bamboos which play to a certain beat or harmony.
Closed accounts, child with P1 million

Security Bank’s Leslie Cham revealed that two checking accounts of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared business interest of the Vice President’s husband, Manases Carpio, were closed last July or the same month when the impeachment trial started.

Lawyer Niña Ferren Aguilar of the Anti-Money Laundering Division of Metropolitan Bank and Trust Company, meanwhile, testified that one of the children of the Duterte-Carpio couple had over P1 million in bank deposits at the end of each year from 2022 to 2025.
Likewise, Aguilar said that their banks’ reporting of suspicious bank transactions to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) is based on news reports and comprehensive evaluation, not gossip.

Ahead of Aguilar’s pronouncement, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura said that the bank accounts under the names of the Vice President and her husband recorded P4.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious bank transactions.
BPI’s Galvez also told the court that the Vice President and her husband have nine bank accounts in the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) with a collective ending balance of P8 million as of 2025.

Galvez said that the nine accounts include the joint accounts of the Vice President and her father, former president Duterte, at the BPI Julia Vargas branch in Pasig City and the BPI Davao Main Branch.

It can be recalled that former senator Trillanes alleged in 2016 that then-Davao City mayor and presidential candidate Rodrigo Duterte and his daughter Sara had millions that he did not declare in his Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.
Galvez said that the Duterte-Carpio couple already closed their 34 accounts in BPI, although he did not say when these accounts were closed.
Bank representatives also said that Vice President Duterte and her husband posted a P39 million ending balance in several bank accounts across eight banks under their names from 2022 to 2025.
The bank officials who made the testimony were from the following financial institutions:

items: Landbank of the Philippines
AUB (Asia United Bank)
PS Bank
Metro Bank
Security Bank
BPI (Bank of the Philippine Islands)
PNB (Philippine National Bank) and
BDO (Banco de Oro)

blocks.text: The 2025 ending balance for the bank accounts of the Vice President and her husband is slightly higher than their 2024 ending balance of P22.2 million.
The 2024 ending balance of P22.2 million, however, was way below their 2023 ending balance which reached P71.3 million.
The 2022 ending balance of the Vice President and her husband, the first year of Duterte in office, amounted to P59 million.
Lawyer Sotero Roman, representative of FWD Life Insurance, also told the Senate court that Carpio bought P10.6 million in investment insurance in 2024.
Roman said that this insurance is already paid for, has a financial value of P13.2 million, and lists the children of the Duterte-Carpio couple as beneficiaries.

Defense counsel CJ Narvasa, in response, cited the provisions of the Insurance Code which state that “the consent of the spouse is not necessary for the validity of an insurance policy taken out by a married person on his or her life or that of his or her children.”

The witnesses from the banks were presented by the prosecution to prove Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President, who amassed unexplained wealth due to alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Maya Turner named 1st female captain in University of Manitoba Bisons football history
articles.summary: Maya Turner just keeps putting the boots to the history books for Canadian university football. The first female to score points in a U Sports football game is now the first female captain in the…

image.caption: Maya Turner has another milestone in her history-making football career as one of the new captains of the University of Manitoba Bisons team. (University of Manitoba/Instagram)

blocks.text: Manitoba

Maya Turner just keeps putting the boots to the history books for Canadian university football. The first female to score points in a U Sports football game is now the first female captain in the century-long history of the Bisons program.
'A huge honour and means a lot that they have that kind of respect': Turner
Maya Turner just keeps putting the boots to the history books for Canadian university football.

The placekicker and punter with the Manitoba Bisons — who became the first woman to score in U Sports football during a pre-season game in 2022 — is now the first female captain in the century-long history of the Bisons football program.

"It's really a huge honour and means a lot that they have that kind of respect for me, just as a player and a teammate, and that they see me as someone who's a leader and has a place on this team regardless of gender," Turner said.
The 24-year-old was named one of the team's seven captains — representing the many different positions — at the end of training camp.
Head coach Stan Pierre announced the names to the team, "and yeah, my name was in there," Turner said, still sounding a bit surprised.
"Yeah, I guess I wasn't totally expecting it."

Maya Turner was the first woman to play and score in a pre-season U Sports football game, then became the first to do it in a regular-season game, and later became the first female Canada West football all-star. (Mike Still/Manitoba Bisons Athletics)
Handing the specialist captaincy to Turner as she enters her senior year was "a pretty easy decision," Pierre said.
"Maya is an exemplary student athlete. She does everything you ask of her, and she does it at a very high level," he said.
"She's a great student, she's a great person, she works extremely hard. She doesn't miss anything and she doesn't make excuses for anything. She just does everything correct.
"I can't think of a better mentor for our young players and a better example as a leader on our football team."
It's possible Turner's the first to break that gender leadership barrier in any Canadian university football program.
"I don't even know how many women have played U Sports [football] — I don't think it's five," Pierre said.
"So I would venture a guess that there's a really good possibility that she is."
Bisons football head coach Stan Pierre says Turner is an exceptional player, period, with no asterisk required because she's female. (University of Manitoba)
Turner first inscribed her name into U Sports history (the national governing body for Canadian university athletics) with her 2022 pre-season boot, but she fully carved it in the following year.
On Sept. 23, 2023, she became the first woman to play and score in a regular-season game, hitting a 21-yard field goal. Then she repeated that distance for the game-winning points in double overtime.
She finished the year with a 79 per cent accuracy mark — third-best percentage in Bison football's century-old history.
One kick was a 48-yarder, the eighth-longest in the nation.

In 2024, her field goal percentage of 75 led the Canada West conference and she hit another one from 48 yards out. Her performance led to her being named a Canada West all-star — another first for women in U Sports football.
She kicked 76 per cent in 2025, including a 15-point contribution on Oct. 18 (four field goals and three extra points) to help the Bisons erase a 10-point deficit and win 33-31.
Turner, who is from Maple Grove, Minn., about 15 kilometres northwest of Minneapolis, played soccer at Loyola University in Chicago before transitioning to kicker with its club football team.
She attended multiple kicking camps in the U.S. and reached out to hundreds of schools to see if any would consider adding her to their men's football team.
"I was just super determined to play this sport at a high level. I knew that I had the abilities, and so I was confident that there would be someone who would be able to recognize that," she said.
She was invited for a tryout with the Bisons and impressed enough to be offered a roster spot.
"Ever since I've been here, I think everyone's done a really good job of just seeing me as football player first and trying to not have me being a woman impact anything," Turner said.

items: Manitoba's Turner to become 1st woman to play in regular-season U Sports football game
Trailblazing University of Manitoba placekicker outboots the men to earn Canada West all-star honours

blocks.text: Pierre agreed, saying the attention Turner gets from outside the Bisons program is understandable, but within the team, she is beloved "not because she's a female but because she's a really good person and a really good player. For us, she's just one of the players.
"It really doesn't feel like anything all that peculiar."

Still, her marks on history are directly linked to her gender, and Pierre hopes Turner has mowed a path for others to follow, though he acknowledged the gender barriers haven't exactly been kicked down.
"I hope she loosened those barriers a little bit and that there is more opportunity. But I'm not naive," he said.
"If there's another female out there that is capable of doing it, I hope that it inspires her. But Maya is a special athlete and what she's done isn't easy.
"She's exceptional to be good enough to compete at this level."

items: Manitoba Bisons kicker Maya Turner hopes to break down barriers for women in sport

articles.title: British Jewish groups to hold London vigil for victims of 7 October attacks
articles.summary:
Gathering expected to take place at Richmond Terrace, opposite Downing Street, at 5pm on Wednesday

British Jewish organisations gathered in central London on Wednesday for a vigil honouring…

blocks.text: British Jewish organisations gathered in central London on Wednesday for a vigil honouring victims of the 7 October attacks in Israel, after a day of tributes from politicians and community leaders.
The vigil took place at Richmond Terrace, opposite Downing Street.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Three years ago, Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel, murdering 1,200 men, women and children, injuring thousands and taking 251 people captive. May their memories for ever remain a blessing.”
Meanwhile, the Jewish Leadership Council said 7 October had been “the deadliest day for our people since the Holocaust”.

The attacks were followed by Israel’s war in Gaza. The Palestinian death toll in the past three years exceeded 74,000 last month, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which is part of the Hamas-led government.
Andy Burnham assured British Jews “we stand with you” against antisemitism, in a statement marking the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks.

However, the Israeli embassy said in a statement: “It is a source of deep sadness that, in the years since 7 October, the position of the British government towards Israel has changed so substantially from the solidarity expressed in those first days,” claiming “the atmosphere for Jewish people continues to worsen” in the UK.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine last month.

The Community Security Trust (CST), which monitors antisemitism, said its research showed there were 1,926 antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK from January to June 2026, up by a fifth on the first half of last year and the second-highest total reported to the CST in the first six months of any year.

blocks.caption: The UK’s chief rabbi, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, and Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, at the vigil in central London. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images

blocks.text: It was exceeded only by the 2,019 incidents recorded in the first half of 2024, which followed the 2023 Hamas attacks and the start of Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza.

Celebrations of Jewish life have been continuing in public spaces. From 27 September to 2 October, the Jewish festival of Sukkot was celebrated in the heart of Manchester, with the Sukkah in the City event in Albert Square.

In his statement, the prime minister described the rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK since 2023 as “disturbing”, but pledged his government was “committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred”.

Burnham referenced an attack just over a year ago on the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur by Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, at Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue in Manchester, which left two worshippers dead.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from stab wounds and his fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors from Al-Shamie. Police shot Al-Shamie dead during the attack.
Burnham said: “Three years on from the 7 October attacks on Israel, we remember those who were senselessly killed by Hamas terrorists.
“The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day.
“In the years since, we have seen a disturbing rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK.

“I want Britain’s Jewish community to hear this from me directly: we stand with you. Abuse and violence against you, in any form, will not be tolerated. Not on our streets, not online, not in our schools or universities.
after newsletter promotion

“That’s why we are funding protection for synagogues, schools and community buildings, and why we will come down hard on antisemitism wherever it is found – in classrooms, on campuses and in neighbourhoods.

“At home, we are committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred. Abroad, we continue to work towards a two-state solution, with Israelis and Palestinians living side-by-side in peace and security.
“An attack on Jewish people in Britain is an attack on all of us. Antisemitism has no place in this country, and we will do everything we can to stamp it out.”

blocks.caption: Protesters outside the University of Edinburgh’s Main Library on Wednesday. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the Metropolitan police said it had “imposed stringent conditions” on those taking part in a pro-Palestine student march in London on Wednesday.

Eleven people were arrested in the capital, including five on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London, the force said.
The Met said the other arrests were made at pro-Palestinian student protests elsewhere in London.
Pro-Palestine protesters also held demonstrations at Edinburgh and Glasgow universities.
Hundreds of people gathered for a rally outside George Square in Edinburgh, outside the University of Edinburgh’s Main Library.
From there they marched to the Bayes Centre – the university’s hub for data science and artificial intelligence – before finishing in the Old College quadrangle.
A similar demonstration was held on Library Hill in Glasgow, outside the university library.
Protesters at both rallies carried Palestinian flags and banners, many bearing slogans about the conflict in Gaza.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey: Could the Mecca defense pact become a game changer in the war against the Houthis in Yemen?
articles.summary: Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to provide "practical measures" to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Could a new alliance reshape the war against the Houthis in Yemen?

image.caption: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia has been fighting against Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in Yemen, as well as launching missiles at Saudi ArabiaImage: Southern Giants Brigades/Handout via REUTERS

blocks.text: The latest iteration of Saudi Arabia's defense deal with Turkey and Pakistan, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, is taking shape amid the country's escalating conflict with Yemen's Houthi militia.

According to the trilateral defense commitment, which was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on August 7, 2026, an armed attack on any one of the three states involved should be regarded as an attack on them all.

Yet, despite ongoing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Saudi attacks on Houthi militants in Yemen, neither Pakistan nor Turkey had joined Saudi Arabia's combat operations since the deal was signed, arguing that the command and operational structures were still being developed.

But since Monday, the situation has changed after an emergency meeting between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey's defense and foreign ministers and senior military chiefs in the Saudi capital Riyadh. According to a joint statement, Turkey and Pakistan decided to implement the collective defense commitments in practical terms immediately. This means providing military forces and capabilities and ensuring their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia. The appointment of a retired Pakistani lieutenant general, Nauman Mahmood, as the alliance's first secretary-general was also announced. He will serve a three-year term.

"Ankara and Islamabad undoubtedly will seek to strengthen the Saudi kingdom's posture vis-a-vis the Houthi threat and demonstrate that the Mecca agreement can pass its first real test and show up as a game-changing alliance," Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, told DW.

"However, what the activation of the Mecca pact means operationally, including the specific capabilities deployed and the scope of their missions, has not been made public," she said, adding that this was "not unusual for such a military operation amid myriad sensitivities."

According to the 2026 Global Firepower military strength ranking, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey between them have about 1.4 million active personnel, some 3,400 military aircraft, 6,000 tanks and more than 340 naval assets.

On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia intercepted another ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Earlier this week, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had launched a large-scale offensive, to recapture territory along the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Mokha. Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes to support the offensive.

blocks.caption: The ministers of the three signatory countries to the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement met in Riyadh on Oct. 5, 2026Image: Mustafa Hatipoglu/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Turkey considers a solution through dialogue

The scope of a potential Turkish military deployment remains unclear. Turkey is a NATO member, which means that any military involvement on its part could carry broader implications for the entire military alliance.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan noted after the meeting in Riyadh on Monday that there were not only military options on the table. "We also discussed what could be done to resolve the problem peacefully and through dialogue,"

Turkey's involvement in the Mecca defense deal has been criticized by opposition parties in the country. Under Turkey's constitution, international agreements generally require approval by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey but this has not yet been granted.

"How can the so-called Mecca agreement on joint defense be valid and implemented without having been submitted to the Turkish parliament for approval?" Namik Tan, an Istanbul lawmaker from the social democratic Yeni Parti and a former Turkish ambassador to Israel and the United States, asked in a statement.
Yani Bagcioglu, a retired Turkish admiral, also warned that "the risk of Turkish forces and commercial vessels linked to Turkey becoming targets of Houthi attacks should not be overlooked."
Pakistan's tightrope walk amid the Iran war

The third signatory, Pakistan, is walking its own particular tightrope. On Monday, Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told Pakistani television channel Geo News that Pakistan and Turkey were playing a "supportive role," with their forces involved in "reconnaissance and other things," while Saudi forces were engaged in combat.

"Pakistan's contribution to the defense of Saudi Arabia is nothing new," Imtiaz Gul, an independent Pakistani security analyst, told DW. "The arrangement has existed for six decades," he said, adding that "defense against the Houthis nevertheless represents a different kind of challenge because the group is considered an Iranian extension and by implication, Iran would consider this an attack on its regional interests."

A direct engagement in Yemen at Saudi Arabia's side would, therefore, risk not only ending Pakistan's apparent neutral status as a mediator in the US-Iran war, but also strain relations with Tehran, he said. He pointed out that Saudi Arabia was a close ally of the US, while the Houthis are backed by Iran.

blocks.caption: Houthi attacks on infrastructure, the East-West oil pipeline and the Saudi capital Riyadh have put pressure on Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to reactImage: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-3/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hisham Al-Omeisy, a Yemeni conflict analyst in Washington, told DW that "for years, a cornerstone of the Houthi narrative and rallying cry has been a fight against perceived external enemies." Accordingly, he added, foreign boots on the ground in Yemen would "not only backfire, it would solidify the Houthi local coalitions and fuel their recruitment drives."
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
Haroon Janjua in Islamabad contributed to this article.
