articles.title: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense | Heather Stewart
articles.summary:
The Tory leader’s proposal to slash the tax would shovel £6bn of taxpayer money to the already-wealthy

Kemi Badenoch’s

blocks.text: Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election.

In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass.
But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early.

So politically, Badenoch’s flagship policy may have merit. IHT, as policymakers call it, is notoriously unpopular. Families never likely to be liable nevertheless fret about their kids having to paying it, while a cacophony of highly paid tax advisers offer to help them avoid it.
The furious response to Rachel Reeves’s reform of the inheritance tax regime for family businesses and farms, with tractors streaming down Whitehall, underlined how unpopular it is.

blocks.caption: Labour’s clash with farmers over inheritance tax prompted eye-catching protests in London. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA

blocks.text: But whatever its political logic, the Tory plan makes little economic sense. First, it’s worth pausing to underline how very wealthy the beneficiaries of this new policy are likely to be.
The latest data from HMRC shows that less than 5% of estates – the wealthiest 5%, that is – were liable for any inheritance tax at all in 2023/24.

And under current rules, by combining their tax-free allowances, a married couple can already pass on a property worth up to £1m to their children or grandchildren, without them being liable to pay a penny in inheritance tax.

Badenoch’s new, much more generous regime would permit a couple to pass on the entire family home, however valuable, without paying any tax on it at all; and for good measure an additional £1m in other assets. And the more valuable the property, the bigger the gain.

Clearly, in a sluggish economy where resources are stretched, there’s a question about whether that is the best use of the £6bn of taxpayers’ money the policy is reckoned to cost – compared with, say, investing in infrastructure where there might be the prospect of a return.
Total revenue from IHT is forecast to be about £9bn this year, rising to £15bn by 2030-31 – Badenoch’s plan would wipe out about half of that.

Worse than that though, it will create perverse incentives for older homeowners to do exactly what the economy needs them not to do, and hang on in a valuable property, for fear the proceeds of downsizing would be grabbed by HMRC .
after newsletter promotion

The Tories claim they’ll also abolish stamp duty, helping to oil the wheels of the property market and encourage downsizing; but for the most valuable homes, the benefits of not paying 40% inheritance tax above the current threshold would be likely to more than overwhelm the boon of a tax-free move.
And that would be likely to mean far fewer family-size homes coming on to the market in the places up-and-coming buyers most need them to be available.
As Arun Advani, of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at the University of Warwick, points out, the biggest beneficiaries would be in areas where housing is expensive.

He says: “‘Where housing is expensive’ mostly means ‘where lots of people want to live’, usually because there are good jobs. Reducing housing sales here will make it harder for young working families trying to upsize. By staying put, they will in turn make it harder for school leavers and university/college graduates to move to the area for work. This is bad for growth,” he said.
Indeed, he points out there would even be an incentive for those who can afford it to “upsize” – moving to a larger house, which would then effectively shelter the asset from inheritance tax.

If Badenoch and her party want to shovel an additional £6bn of taxpayers’ money to the already-wealthy in the hope of winning back votes in the stockbroker belt, so be it – but she should not be able to claim the policy would be anything but bad for economic growth.

articles.title: Russia: WHO not able to 'fully' assess plague situation
articles.summary: The UN health agency said Russia should be more transparent about the case of the plague as reports of a second case of the disease emerged. Russia played down any concerns, saying the population…

image.caption: A second case of the disease was reported in connection with the anti-plague center in IrkutskImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: The World Health Organization (WHO) said it could not fully assess the situation of the suspected plague death of a laboratory employee in Russia.
"We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov played down the reports as "false information," insisting only Russian authorities' official statements should be relied on.

Peskov also said he had no information regarding a planned call between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation, despite Trump announcing such a call was scheduled.
The US did make a formal request for more information on the matter from Russia, the AFP news agency reported.
Second suspected case reported
This comes after a 28-year-old female technician employed at a plague research institute in the Irkutsk region of Siberia died of the disease, possibly contracting it from a broken test tube.
According to the WHO head, Russia should clarify reports of a "second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause" at the institute.
While the United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Moscow to be transparent about the case, Russian authorities insist the population in the region is safe.

blocks.caption: WHO head  Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for more transparency from RussiaImage: World Health Organization/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "There are no epidemic risks for the population," the country's health agency said, adding its investigations had resulted in "no emergencies" and emphasizing the plague research institute's compliance.
"More than 90 percent of contacts have completed medical observation," the agency added. "The results of almost 5,000 laboratory tests did not reveal any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms."
In response to the reports, Mongolia said it implemented "health surveillance and monitoring measures" at the border between the two countries.
Could a Russia plague case trigger wider concern?

articles.title: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation
articles.summary:
Internal inquiry clears Dan Jukes and James Orr, who were filmed talking about scheme involving US donor

Reform UK has cleared two senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign…

blocks.text: Reform UK has cleared two senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation.
The party published a 27-page report of an internal inquiry finding that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s press adviser, and James Orr, its head of policy, had not breached funding rules.
Party sources said they intended to pursue legal action against the undercover reporting group Verbatim, whose footage led to the investigation and was broadcast by Channel 4 News.

However, Labour said the report was a “whitewash” given it was undertaken by the party’s legal secretary, Adam Richardson, a barrister with a longstanding association with the party, and Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary. Labour also said it was not credible for the party to distance itself from the scandal by claiming Orr and Jukes, two of Farage’s top team, were just contractors.

Police have been investigating potential offences under electoral law since the broadcast in early September, saying they would widen an existing special inquiry relating to donations made to Reform. Jukes and Orr will remain suspended by the party while the police inquiry continues.

Jukes and Orr were filmed talking about a scheme in which a US donor paid for three polls with favourable narratives for Reform, costing more than £30,000. Donations from overseas sources are not allowed under political funding laws.
Jukes also discussed the idea of the US donor giving £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son. The men they thought were father and son were undercover reporters.
Farage later met the undercover reporters as would-be donors over lunch in Clacton, and did not object when the idea of the scheme was explained to him. He later said he had not been listening.

In its internal report, Reform said it did not excuse the “foolish” way in which Jukes and Orr discussed donations with an overseas donor. But it said the party had not commissioned the £30,000 polling from the US donor, as Jukes was a contractor rather than a staff member.

Orr was recorded suggesting the US businessman could pay for opinion polling to help with the party’s campaigns, which would “technically be a donation in kind” but “the reality is we could easily get away with it”.

However, the internal report found that because Reform did not make any payment for the polls or directly arrange for them to be carried out, “the payments made to JL Partners were therefore not donations to Reform UK within the meaning of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000”.

In relation to discussions about the £500,000, which was never handed over, the report said it found no evidence that Orr or Jukes knowingly entered into or acted in furtherance of an arrangement to facilitate an impermissible donation.

The report said: “Nothing was agreed, no donations were made and no formal position was presented to the party’s finance team, and nothing was accepted. The party’s procedures for checking the identity of a donor and the source of funds were never engaged, because nothing reached them.”

Orr had also told the undercover reporter: “If there’s a non-trivial chance of you guys directly giving a … five or six-figure sum, then we could do a lunch with Nigel.” The report said “the words used were unwise” but concluded that “they were not a price”.

It also dismissed an incident in which Jukes discussed other purported foreign donors who had given money through their children, which would be against the rules. Jukes insisted “he simply invented circumstances for the purposes of not derailing the conversation” and that it was “foolish, loose talk” without foundation.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Dan Jukes, left, with Farage in Clacton in 2024. Jukes said he would ‘continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities’. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters

blocks.text: The investigation “found no basis for the suggestion that any supporter of the party has given in the way described”. As a result of the episode, which overshadowed Reform’s conference in early September, the party said it would bring in rules that the party treasurer’s office must be informed in writing of proposed donations and that no meetings with proposed donors should take place until background checks had been carried out.
But Labour’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, said “nothing in it exonerates Reform or Nigel Farage from the serious allegations that they still face”.
“The scandals and multiple police investigations aren’t going away. It’s time to stop the desperate deflection and cover ups,” she added.
A Reform spokesperson said: “Following the allegations raised by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 on 3 September, Reform UK commissioned a comprehensive internal investigation.
“The investigation examined all relevant evidence, including witness interviews, documentary records and electronic communications.
“Having concluded the review, the investigation found no evidence that any laws were broken. Reform UK takes its obligations on governance and conduct extremely seriously.
“We consider that the production company – Verbatim – acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course.”

Jukes told the Telegraph, which first reported the findings of the internal investigation: “I welcome the finding of this investigation, which crucially has found I did not break the law, as I have maintained from the outset.
“I am also considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me.
“For now, I will continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities.”

A spokesperson for Verbatim said: “We note that this report is an internal one authored by Reform’s own barrister and general secretary, and that a police investigation remains ongoing. We are confident in our journalism, which speaks for itself.”

articles.title: German court orders detention of former intelligence chief after spying arrest
articles.summary:
August Hanning, 80, appears before judge after being accused of treason and espionage on behalf of foreign state

A formal arrest warrant has been issued against Germany’s former top spy,…

blocks.text: A formal arrest warrant has been issued against Germany’s former top spy, with a judge ordering him to be held in pre-trial detention, a day after he was arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency.
August Hanning, 80, is accused of buying secret documents from a former colleague and using them to advise a foreign intelligence service, according to the office of the federal prosecutor.

Hanning’s arrest on Tuesday, along with that of his former office head, referred to as Manfred D. It has sent shock waves through Germany’s political and intelligence community, with analysts calling it potentially the country’s biggest espionage scandal since the end of the cold war.

It has raised questions in Berlin over how Germany’s foreign intelligence service can uphold its reputation internationally, particularly at a time of heightened security concerns. Also under scrutiny is the sustainability of rules governing the conduct of retired senior officials and their ability to earn extra income based on their insider knowledge and professional networks.
Hanning was head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service (BND) between 1998 and 2005.

A lawyer for Hanning denied he had been involved in any wrongdoing on Wednesday, telling the conservative daily newspaper Die Welt: “While it is true that he ‌was in possession of confidential documents, the allegation that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of Germany, let alone for payment, is incorrect.”
Manfred D, who was also placed under formal arrest on Wednesday by the judge in Karlsruhe, has yet to respond to questions via his lawyer.

Hanning is alleged to have agreed in 2010 to pay for information from Manfred D, who allegedly then smuggled it out of the BND. Manfred D, 64, had worked under Hanning and went on to serve subsequent BND bosses after Hanning, before retiring in March this year.

blocks.caption: Members of the media attempt to take a photograph of Hanning as he is driven away from court on Wednesday. Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPA

blocks.text: Hanning is believed to have received about 2,000 documents from Manfred D until June 2022, some of which were classified, according to prosecutors. He is alleged to have used the information in his papers for his private consulting work.

Prosecutors were alerted to Hanning’s alleged criminal activities by investigators gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which the former spy chief is accused of participating in using his former contacts with Israeli intelligence. Christina Block, an heiress to the business, allegedly paid Hanning and a retired police officer more than €100,000 (£85,000) for their roles in the alleged abduction of her two children from her ex-husband.

A report in Der Spiegel on Wednesday said investigators were looking into a possible connection to the foreign intelligence service of Azerbaijan as one of the agencies Hanning may have been passing information to.

Azerbaijan’s media and broadcasting council denied any connection to Hanning or the investigation. “The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations,” the council said in a statement.

The scandal has awakened memories of the Günter Guillaume affair, when an East German Stasi spy and his wife posing as refugees infiltrated the government of the then chancellor Willy Brandt, leading to Brandt’s resignation in 1974.

Marc Henrichmann, the head of the parliamentary committee overseeing the intelligence services, which has repeatedly raised questions about the post-career consulting activities of intelligence agency employees but has been told legal obstacles stood in the way of challenging them, said he was “fairly flabbergasted” by the affair, but stressed it was as yet unclear the breadth and extent of the alleged wrongdoing.
“As yet we don’t know exactly what happened,” he told the public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk, while acknowledging the need to “restore broken trust” in the BND.

blocks.caption: Police officers stand outside Hanning’s home in Nordwalde on Tuesday after his arrest. Photograph: Christoph Reichwein/DPA/AP

blocks.text: On Wednesday, politicians and intelligence analysts called for stricter regulation around allowing former security employees to make use of their influence and knowledge after retiring.

The scandal comes at a time when Germany is attempting to make its intelligence agencies, including the BND and its domestic sibling, the BfV, more robust, efficient and independent from those of its allies, in particular boosting their powers of surveillance to more effectively tackle sabotage and hacking attacks, amid rising threats from external powers such as Russia and Iran.

The scandal is yet another blow to the BND’s reputation. Not only is it notoriously dependent on information from foreign agencies to foil terror attacks on German soil, but it has faced other cases of its staff allegedly spying for other countries.
It has also been reeling from the case of a department head, Carsten L, who was accused in December 2022 of spying for Russia. His trial is now being heard by Berlin’s higher regional court.
Sensitivities over the country’s past, when dictatorships misused their powers of surveillance to spy on their own people, have made reform of the agencies hard to pursue.

Hanning, the son of a brickyard owner, rose through the ranks of the intelligence service to become its head. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, he oversaw the investigation into some of the terrorists who had studied in Hamburg. He initiated wide-reaching reforms of the BND including bringing it closer to politics, becoming a close adviser to the then interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble. He spoke out against a “culture of leaks” and was deeply critical of the NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden, calling him an “internal offender”.

Once his civil service career was over, Hanning continued to hold a role as a respected behind-the-scenes negotiator, and frequently intervened in government security policy debates. At the same time he built up his consultant business, founding an agency with his wife, Ruth, called Hanning Consult, and worked for various other global consulting agencies. He even produced a “spy cookbook” with his wife, called “Top(f) Secret” (Topf being the German word for saucepan).

articles.title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
articles.summary: People with mental illness alone were to be eligible for assisted dying in Canada in March 2027, but that has now been paused indefinitely.

blocks.text: Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.
It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.
On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time".
Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to healthcare.
A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.
Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future.
Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.
The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said.

That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so.
However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces.
Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses.
"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.
Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.
Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent. In Canada, that mechanism is known as "track two" Maid.
Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.
Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness.

Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that euthanasia would offer her "a safe death".
But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility.
"When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said.

Some experts have also raised concerns more broadly that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort.

In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying.
It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services".

The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium.
Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased".
Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support access, external to medically assisted death but that support falls it comes to patients with mental illness alone.

items: If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.
In Canada, support can be found at the Suicide Crisis Helpline by dialling 988

articles.title: Sara Duterte, Rodrigo's P96-M joint deposits should appear in SALN --Gatchalian
articles.summary: The joint deposits of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, amounting to P96 million should have been reflected in the former's Statement of Assets,…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 12:46am

The joint deposits of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, amounting to P96 million should have been reflected in the former's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net worth (SALN), Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Wednesday.

During the Senate impeachment trial, Bank of the Philippine Islands Central Metro Manila Branches Division Head Marwin Galvez confirmed that the father and daughter opened joint time deposit accounts worth P40 million and P55 million in 2010.
Public prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said the P40-million deposit had grown to P41.72 million by the time it matured in March 2011, bringing the combined value of the accounts to P96 million.

"Binabangga ko ito sa SALN ni Vice President at kung merong time deposit na joint account na P96 million, dapat mag-reflect iyan sa SALN niya. I'm looking at the 2010 SALN, wala akong makitang P96 million, and sa 2011," Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said in his interjection.

(I’m comparing this with the Vice President’s SALN. If she had a joint time deposit account worth P96 million, it should have been reflected in her SALN. I’m looking at her 2010 SALN, and I can’t find P96 million there, nor in her 2011 SALN.)

Alih said the funds were later used to purchase manager’s checks starting in 2011, in response to Gatchalian’s questions about how the money was transferred from the joint accounts to pay for the checks.

"Dito sa 2011, wala rin akong makitang P96M, then sinabi mo kanina sa 2012 wala na. I'm trying to link iyong sinasabi niyo na bumili ng manager's check, nilagay muna sa account ng bank at nagiging unutilized yung manager's check. I'm trying to link that to the SALN and see if there is a pattern," Gatchalian said.

(Similarly, I couldn't find the P96 million in her 2011 SALN, and you said earlier it was no longer there in 2012. I’m trying to link your testimony that the funds were used to purchase manager’s checks, deposited back into the bank, and eventually became unutilized checks, with the SALNs to see if there is a pattern.)
Defense counsel Michael Poa said the "operative phrase" was "if she (Sara Duterte) was aware about the deposits.
"All these time deposits, transactions did not have the signature of the Vice President and all of them were done by former president Rodrigo Duterte, we leave it at that," Poa said.

Gatchalian replied saying, "That’s why I'm asking kung if there was a need for the vice president to appear for the signature card. As early as 2010, the vice president had a signature in the joint account; apparently she has."
Poa said it was for this reason that the defense panel was asking for the updating of the account.
"But again, I don't want to cross the line and will leave it to the appreciation of the court," he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Gerhard Schröder visits latest Russian employer, Hyperglobus
articles.summary: Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder visited a Moscow supermarket in his new role on the supervisory board. Schröder is no stranger to retirement stipends in Russia — or the scandal that…

image.caption: Schröder's various board positions in Russia, not least at state energy giants, have caused considerable controversy in recent years, particularly since the full-scale invasion of UkraineImage: RBC/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Gerhard Schröder visited one of the Moscow branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain on Wednesday, a few days after being named a member of its supervisory board.
Russian TV footage showed employees at the branch greeting the former German chancellor and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, with sustained applause.

Schröder has current or recent links to a series of Russian businesses and to President Vladimir Putin, issues that have become increasingly contentious in Germany in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

blocks.caption: Schröder was German chancellor when Vladimir Putin first became Russian president; the pair have remained close since he left office, despite all that followedImage: Alexei Druzhinin/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is Hyperglobus' link to Germany?
The new Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus was spun off from Germany's Globus Holding last year.

Last week, Hyperglobus announced that Schröder had been appointed to the supervisory board. The supermarket confirmed that the former chancellor and Social Democrat had visited a branch on the western outskirts of Moscow on Wednesday.
"I'm very pleased to be here, to see this wonderful hypermarket, to see the results of your work and to meet you, my wonderful colleagues," RBC television in Russia quoted Schröder as saying.

blocks.caption: Schröder and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, were greeted with sustained applause, Russian TV reportedImage: RBC/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Schröder also reportedly called last week for the continuation of remaining trade ties between Russia and countries like Germany amid the sanctions imposed since the start of the war in Ukraine.
"It is exactly in these crisis times that these ties are especially important: they allow us to hear each other and look for ways forward," newspaper RBK reported him as saying last Friday.
What's the deal with Schröder, Putin, Russia and Ukraine?

Schröder's close ties to Putin came under scrutiny even while he was still in office, not least in 2004 when Schröder responded to a question from a reporter by saying that, yes, he believed Putin was a "flawless democrat" or lupenreiner Demokrat.
Even 22 years ago, this assertion strained credulity in many eyes — not least among opposition groups or in war-torn Chechnya.

On leaving politics, Schröder kept close ties to the Kremlin and took up a series of senior roles, perhaps most famously on the board of the Rosneft energy giant and before that on the board of the Nord Stream gas pipeline project that was majority owned by Gazprom.

blocks.caption: Putin has often said Schröder could negotiate a peace deal with Ukraine. Schröder, in turn, has declared himself willing.Image: Vladimir Rodionov/Ria Novosti/Kremlin Pool/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In 2014, not long after the annexation of Crimea and as a Russian-backed civil war brewed in Ukraine, Schröder was Nord Stream's guest of honor in St. Petersburg, where he celebrated his 70th birthday in lavish style.

Four years later, after an election many in the West decried as bordering on a sham, Schröder took a prominent place at the 2018 swearing-in ceremony for Putin's fourth presidential term at the Kremlin (pictured above).
Now-deceased Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny once said Schröder was Putin's "errand boy."

In 2024, Schröder was stripped of a state-funded office and staff — typically provided to former chancellors — on the basis that he was no longer fulfilling any obligations tied to his previous role in government.

His party, the center-left Social Democrats, tried on several occasions to eject him as a member. Each attempt failed to clear the high legal bars required, and he remains a member, having joined in 1963.

Putin has often suggested him as a possible peace mediator between Russia, Ukraine and Europe — with Schröder also expressing a willingness to take on the role — even though the reality is he would likely be entirely unacceptable as a mediator to all parties other than Russia, and particularly to Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia bombed apartment block as birthday gift for Putin
articles.summary:
Building in Pryluky destroyed, killing nine people including three children, officials say, night before Russian president’s 74th birthday

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia’s military…

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia’s military of deliberately killing civilians and bombing residential buildings as a macabre gift for Vladimir Putin, who celebrates his 74th birthday on Wednesday.
Ukraine’s president described Russia’s overnight drone and missiles strikes, which killed at least 24 people, as “despicable”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said.

Video showed a ballistic missile slamming into a five-storey apartment block in the town of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The concrete building collapsed, entombing those inside. Eighteen people died, including four children, officials said.

Zelenskyy identified them as Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, who was one year old, as well as eight-year-old Maksym. He said five children were among about 50 people who were injured. Rescuers continued to pick through the rubble, with several residents not yet accounted for, he added.

“Today, on Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘presented’ him with the destruction of a residential block in Pryluky,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “The Russians know very well that they are striking ordinary cities, ordinary life. It is an absolutely deliberate choice of terror.”

He acknowledged Ukraine was struggling to shoot down enemy ballistic missiles, and appealed to allies to provide US-manufactured Patriot interceptors. “Air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” he said.

blocks.caption: People carry a casualty after the attack on Pryluky. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: The bombardment featured 70 ballistic missiles, as well as 46 jet-powered drones, which in recent weeks have been terrorising Ukrainians on a daily basis. Ukraine’s air force said it managed to down more than 80% of the fast-moving drones – an improvement on the previous average of 50% to 60%.

Eleven regions were hit. Two people were killed in Kyiv, with other deadly strikes in the central cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia, where four civilians died. There was also extensive damage in Dnipro.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian generals had given Putin his favourite birthday present: “war crimes”. Moscow’s grim strategy of bombarding the country’s population so it capitulated would not work, he said.

“The Ukrainian people are not going to give up, because it’s about Ukraine’s survival as a nation and as a state,” he said. The “ultimate” present would be a dock in The Hague, home to the international criminal court, where the Russian president would stand trial, Sybiha said.

One resident in Kremenchuk said the attack happened early on Wednesday. The woman told Ukrainian media: “We were making tea in the morning. My husband was getting ready for work. And that was it. I found myself on the floor. What can I say? It was very scary.”

Local people in Dnipro said a blast wave affected 16 buildings, blowing out doors and windows. One woman, Iryna, said her auto parts workshop had been hit for the sixth time. The ceiling collapsed in Wednesday’s strike, she said, with toilets, sinks and equipment damaged.

“The explosion happened around three in the morning. We were sleeping at home. Everyone was scared, probably the whole city heard it. We will restore the shop and continue to work,” she told the Suspline channel.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine had carried out its own long-range strikes on economic and military sites inside Russia. They included two oil complexes and a training ground in the ⁠Perm, ​Samara ‌and Astrakhan ‌regions.“These are ‌justified Ukrainian responses to ​all Russian attacks on ⁠our people,” ​he said.

The president posted dramatic video of a burning oil tanker close to the southern resort city of Sochi. Russian officials said naval drones had hit the Liberian-flagged ship, adding that “crude oil was burning openly on the Black Sea”. Its Indian crew of 23 was rescued, they said.

Both sides have heavily targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since Putin’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In recent weeks Russia has picked off vessels carrying Ukrainian grain, paralysing maritime traffic from Ukraine’s southern ports including Odesa.

Earlier this week, a civilian cargo ship sank after a suspected attack by Russian drones in the Black Sea. Its crew is still missing. A second vessel carrying grain was also hit while sailing in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, said the Bulgarian prime minister, Rumen Radev. The search for survivors was called off on Wednesday, according to Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration Executive ⁠Agency. “There are no ​traces of the sailors from the ‌first ship, and there will ‌be none,” he said.

articles.title: Former UBC professor tells defamation trial he was 'shocked' by sexual assault accusation
articles.summary: Author and former UBC professor Steven Galloway says he was "shocked" to learn he was being accused of sexual assault, and believed he had split amicably after an affair with the former student…

image.caption: Author and former UBC professor Steven Galloway is seen through a window as he leaves B.C. Supreme Court during a break at his defamation lawsuit, in Vancouver, on Oct. 6. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Author and former UBC professor Steven Galloway says he was "shocked" to learn he was being accused of sexual assault, and believed he had split amicably after an affair with the former student making the allegation.
Steven Galloway told Vancouver court he believed he had split 'amicably' with former student after affair

Galloway told a B.C. Supreme Court judge in his lawsuit alleging defamation that the relationship was "inappropriate, ill-advised and stupid," but they'd maintained a friendship and regular contact after they split in 2013.

His legal action alleges the woman, whose identity is protected by a publication ban, and others repeated the allegations online and defamed him, setting off the loss of his job at the university as a professor and chair of the creative writing department.

Galloway testified he'd had a two-year consensual relationship with A.B., a former student who was older than him, whom he'd met sometime in 2011 when she took a writing course from a colleague of his.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins

He told the court that he'd learned of the sexual assault allegation while he was in Ohio for an event in November 2015, and spoke with Annabel Lyon, who was acting chair of the creative writing department in his absence.

He says Lyon kept asking if he was suicidal, then police showed up to his hotel room on a report that he was a danger to himself and others, and he was handcuffed and committed to a psychiatric hospital for 72 hours.
"I kept saying to her, 'no, I'm fine.' At one point, I said, 'Annabel, don't worry. I'm way too much of a coward to kill myself,' and that's the kind of sense of humour I have."
"The next thing I know, there's a knock on my door, and it's the police."

items: Steven Galloway defamation trial begins in B.C. Supreme Court
Defendant apologizes to B.C. writer days before defamation trial to start

blocks.text: Galloway said he didn't know where he was or what was happening, and "then I got put in the most terrifying place I've ever been in my life."
Earlier in the hearing on Tuesday, Galloway's wife testified that her husband was "gutted" after being accused of rape, and became extremely distraught as he repeatedly denied the allegations.
Katie Wagner told the court that before Galloway was accused of sexual assault, suspended, then fired from his teaching position, he was extroverted and socially active in the literary community.
She said he stopped playing piano and reading and writing after his career was derailed by the allegations, that would resurface repeatedly online after he was suspended in November 2015.

"He lost his writing career when he was accused of sexual assault, when every single time we tried to put out a different sort of thing, somebody came back and said that it was a sexual assault," she said.
"His whole world was about the Canadian literary community."
Galloway is pictured in his former office at UBC in Vancouver on March 31, 2014. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
Justice Neena Sharma began the second day of the trial in Vancouver by granting continued anonymity to the defendant in the long-running defamation case, first filed in 2018.

The judge said A.B. has shown that identifying her would carry objective harms and specific risks, and allowing anonymity is in line with protecting the privacy and dignity of sexual assault complainants.

Sharma said the woman has withdrawn her defence of her statements against Galloway as justified, but has not admitted that her accusations are false and the court can’t make assumptions until it hears all evidence.
The court heard on Monday that the woman received hateful and vitriolic messages after she was identified in news articles related to the author’s lawsuit.
A.B. had sought an indefinite order to keep her identity under a publication ban, but Sharma's order will expire within six weeks of a ruling in the case, although she can apply to extend it.

Sharma said A.B. is not participating in the trial due to her fragile mental state, which has included suicide attempts, though she's shown "resilience" dealing with past proceedings before the trial.
The court has heard from both Galloway's and A.B.'s lawyers about their clients' mental health struggles, including suicide attempts, in the years since the accusations became public.
Galloway’s lawsuit was originally filed against numerous defendants who allegedly defamed him online and in other forums by repeating unproven allegations of rape.
The court has heard that four defendants remain.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here’s where to look for help:

items: Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
This guide from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health outlines how to talk about suicide with someone you're worried about.

articles.title: German politicians warn of antisemitism on October 7 anniversary
articles.summary: Leading German politicians including Chancellor Merz and President Steinmeier called for people to reject antisemitism.

image.caption: Demonstrations were held across Germany commemorating victims of the October 7 attacksImage: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

blocks.text: High-ranking German politicians marked the anniversary of the terrorist attacks that took place in Israel on October 7, 2023.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke about doing more to fight antisemitism within Germany, while also pressing for a two-state solution between Israelis and Palestinians.
"We are witnessing rising antisemitism in Germany — antisemitism that far too often goes unchallenged," Merz said, adding that his government "will do everything" to combat it.

"Jewish people must be able to live without fear throughout Germany," Merz said in a statement, also emphasizing Germany's support for Israel. "Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime never happens again."
'Political action' needed
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said antisemitism in Germany "flared up in an intolerable manner since October 7."

"Germany must continue to stand up against antisemitism and for Israel’s security, for the dignity and self-determination of the Palestinians, and for the prospect of peaceful coexistence in the Middle East," he said in a statement.
Federal Parliamentary Speaker Julia Klöckner commemorated the day by emphasizing that more needs to be done to combat antisemitism through "political action."
"Antisemitism should not be allowed to have a place on our streets or our political debates," she said.

blocks.caption: Germany Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Israel in December 2025Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany stands with Israel

Some 1,200 people were killed in the attack, carried out by Palestinian militant group Hamas and its affiliates, while 251 people were kidnapped to Gaza, in the deadliest attack on Jews since the end of the Holocaust.
More than 74,000 people have been killed in the Gaza Strip in Israel's war following the attack, with some countries and human rights groups saying Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians.
Demonstrations were held across Germany for victims of both the Hamas attacks and the Israeli war that followed.

In Berlin, a crowd of around 1,700 people, many waving Israeli flags, gathered at Bebelplatz, according to police estimates. Israeli Ambassador Ron Prosor and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt also attended. Bebelplatz was the site of Nazi book burnings following the party's seizure of power in 1933.

Germany has supported Israel throughout the war, although Merz did halt of delivery of some military equipment to Israel following growing legal concerns over the war in Gaza, including arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.
Although Germany is a party to the treaty that created the ICC, Merz vowed not to arrest Netanyahu should he travel to Germany.

articles.title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
articles.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has refused to take any personal responsibility for what happened or order a state inquiry.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Residents of Kfar Aza attended a memorial ceremony on Wednesday for those killed on 7 October 2023
ByLucy Williamson
Middle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem and Kfar Aza
As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.

It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.
The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.
"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.

The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.
Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.

And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.
"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, More than 60 residents of Kfar Aza were killed by Hamas-led gunmen and 19 were taken hostage three years ago

blocks.text: More than 60 residents of Kfar Aza were killed by Hamas-led gunmen and 19 were taken hostage three years ago

Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.
For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.
Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.

"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened – not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."
"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected any personal responsibility for security failures three years ago

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected any personal responsibility for security failures three years ago
Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours – which he denies.

Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.

Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.
Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".

Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.
"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.
"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Netanyahu denied reports that he was warned by the UAE's president days before Hamas attacked

blocks.text: Netanyahu denied reports that he was warned by the UAE's president days before Hamas attacked
Yaacov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.

In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.
He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.
"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."
But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.

"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israelis have held protests to demand the establishment of a state commission of inquiry

blocks.text: Israelis have held protests to demand the establishment of a state commission of inquiry
For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.
A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie".
"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."
Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.
He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.
Netanyahu has so far rejected any personal responsibility for the attacks.

Col Richard Hecht was the IDF's international spokesman on 7 October. He told me the refusal of political leaders - including Netanyahu - to accept responsibility was part of the reason he resigned six months later.

"It's a disgrace," he told me. "When you look at accountability, within the IDF I don't think there's a problem. And that's the pain. That's one of the main causes of bad blood between the political echelon and the military."
At a memorial ceremony in Jerusalem on Monday, the father of one of those killed on 7 October stood up to challenge the prime minister.
"You didn't protect my son, you didn't protect all those who were murdered," he said, before security guards led him away. "Shame! Disgrace!"

blocks.caption: Image caption, "Netanyahu does not surrender" is a slogan of his right-wing Likud party

blocks.text: "Netanyahu does not surrender" is a slogan of his right-wing Likud party
Three years on from the attacks, calls for accountability are growing. Campaigners have asked Israel's highest court to force the government into establishing a state commission of inquiry.
Yizhar Shai, a former minister and opposition politician whose youngest son Yaron, a soldier, was killed on 7 October, is part of that campaign.

"We are going into these elections almost blindfolded as it relates to October 7th," he told me during a protest in Tel Aviv last week. "Our prime minister has never given a detailed, thorough explanation under oath, where he would be asked all the tough questions and have to explain everything."
Netanyahu has consistently refused a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Before calling an election, his government proposed an alternative "national commission of inquiry", whose members would be appointed by political parties.
But despite passing a raft of other legislation before parliament ended its session in July, Israel's government said it ran out of time to pass a bill setting out its plans for the inquiry.
We approached several members of his Likud party for an interview, without success. We also requested that the party respond to their critics, and are waiting for their response.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gadi Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have backed calls for a state commission of inquiry

blocks.text: Gadi Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have backed calls for a state commission of inquiry
Netanyahu's denial of responsibility has now become an election issue, as he prepares to run for re-election later this month.

A video game called Sleepy Bibi, released by the team of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, asks players to help the prime minister avoid responsibility by dodging warnings of an attack and "making it to bed safely".
Netanyahu has styled himself for decades as Israel's "Mr Security", and despite presiding over the worst security failure in Israel's history, is running on the same security platform again.
For the past three years, he focused on waging new wars against Israel's enemies - Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
Polls suggest a close race, and that the 7 October attacks are central to many voters' decisions.
Yaacov Katz says the legacy of 7 October is a coin with two sides.

"There are the failures, the mistakes that led to the Hamas invasion," he told me. "But there's the other side, which is Netanyahu's argument; that [he] has re-engineered the Middle East and made Israel a safer place today. And that is an argument Israelis take with them to the polls."
The shadow of the attacks hangs over this election, dividing Israel once again along political lines.
For supporters, it confirms that Benjamin Netanyahu is still needed to keep Israel safe.
Critics say his political survival puts Israel at risk.

articles.title: Stronger primary, preventive care for Pinoys sought
articles.summary: Sen. Bong Go has urged the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. to further strengthen primary and preventive health care while ensuring adequate benefits for Filipinos undergoing dialysis and other…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am
PhilHealth acting president and CEO Dr. Beverly Ho said roughly P100 billion out of about P400 billion in total disbursements accounts for dialysis.
Businessworld / File

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Bong Go has urged the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. to further strengthen primary and preventive health care while ensuring adequate benefits for Filipinos undergoing dialysis and other life-sustaining treatments following PhilHealth’s disclosure that around 25 percent of its payouts goes to dialysis.
She stressed that earlier management of hypertension and diabetes could help prevent kidney disease from progressing to the point that patients require regular dialysis.
Go said the figures underscore the need to invest more aggressively in keeping Filipinos healthy before illnesses become severe and more difficult to treat.
“Let us take care of our health while it’s early and not wait for the condition to worsen, including hypertension and diabetes,” Go said.
He stressed that efforts to prevent chronic kidney disease should not come at the expense of patients who already depend on dialysis.
“To those needing dialysis, support must be sustained. We are talking about lives here. We should not hold back on spending for health care,” he said.
Go said PhilHealth funds should be maximized for the direct benefit of its members, particularly ordinary Filipinos who often struggle with health care expenses.
“PhilHealth funds are the people’s money, from their contributions. We must return it to them through quality health care,” Go said.
“Every peso, every centavo. It’s their money,” he added.

Go had strongly opposed the transfer of PhilHealth funds to the National Treasury and welcomed the return of P60 billion following a Supreme Court ruling, reiterating that money intended for health care must remain for the health needs of Filipinos. The high court unanimously ordered the return of the transferred amount and permanently prohibited the transfer of the remaining P29.9 billion.

Ho described PhilHealth’s investment in primary care as a strategic approach to the long-term sustainability of the national health insurance fund, pointing out that dialysis can also affect patients’ ability to work because treatment requires regular sessions.

articles.title: DepEd to include mathematics in ARAL program expansion
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) will expand its Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning Program to include Mathematics in an effort to sustain gains in the Program for International Student…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am
This file photo shows a facade of the Department of Education.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) will expand its Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program to include Mathematics in an effort to sustain gains in the Program for International Student Assessment 2025.“The latest PISA results showed us that real progress is possible when we focus on foundational skills, but it also served as a clear reminder of how much ground we still need to cover,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said.
Under DepEd Memorandum 060, Series of 2026, the ARAL Mathematics program aims to improve core numeracy skills among learners from Grades 1 to 10.

“With ARAL Mathematics, our goal is simple: to reach every learner, wherever they are in their learning journey. Whether a child needs help recognizing basic numbers or mastering algebraic concepts, we are building a system that gives them targeted, flexible support so no learner gets left behind,” Angara said.
The program will address learning gaps through diagnostic profiling using the Rapid Mathematics Assessment.
Tutors will track learners’ progress through an Individual Mathematics Intervention Plan to provide tailored support.

“Reading opens the door to knowledge, while mathematics builds the logic and critical thinking our youth need for the future. By combining structured practice with flexible scheduling, we are ensuring our schools have the tools to turn early learning wins into lasting academic resilience,” Angara said.
Under the guidelines, tutoring groups must maintain a ratio of 10 to 15 learners per tutor to maximize individual attention.
Instruction will prioritize self-paced learning, allowing learners to work independently through structured worksheets while tutors serve as facilitators rather than traditional lecturers.
Nationwide implementation in all public schools will begin in the second term of the school year 2026-2027.

articles.title: Marcos to agencies: Prioritize food, fuel, electricity
articles.summary: President Marcos is zeroing in on efforts to ensure enough food, fuel and electricity supply after inflation soared to 7.2 percent last month due to the Middle East conflict and recent disasters,…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am

SINGAPORE – President Marcos is zeroing in on efforts to ensure enough food, fuel and electricity supply after inflation soared to 7.2 percent last month due to the Middle East conflict and recent disasters, Malacañang said.
Palace press officer Claire Castro said Marcos met with Executive Secretary Ralph Recto yesterday to discuss ways to ease the impact of rising prices.

“We are preparing for this. We cannot deny the effect of the ongoing crisis in the Middle East and the calamities that entered the Philippines. Even the political noise is affecting our economy,” Castro said.

“The President is now focusing on food, fuel and electricity. The directive of the President is to ensure that the Philippines will not run out of fuel supply. If the supply of fuel is disrupted, businesses would be disrupted and it would have a bigger effect on our economy,” she added.
Inflation quickened to 7.2 percent in September from 6.1 percent in August and 1.7 in the same month last year mainly due to higher food and energy prices.
Rice inflation accelerated due to tighter domestic supply and higher transportation costs.
Fish and vegetable inflation quickened due to weather disturbances that affected supply.
Castro gave assurance that the government will sustain policies and programs designed to assist vulnerable sectors.

She cited the removal of the 12-percent value added tax in the allowable system loss charge in electricity bills; the management of pork supply during the holiday season; the UPLIFT program, which involves interventions that aid sectors hit by the impact of the Middle East war; the TUPAD emergency employment program and free rice program. “The fuel subsidy for PUV (public utility vehicle) drivers will continue as well as the expansion of Kadiwa,” Castro said, referring to the program for accessible and affordable goods.
Castro said the government is also bracing for the effects of El Niño, which started this month and may last until March next year.
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III and Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida will serve as caretakers while Marcos is out of the country.

articles.title: 80% of Pinoy children face violence – CEAP
articles.summary: Eighty percent of Filipino children have experienced some form of violence at home, school, workplace, community or in dating relationships, the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am
A child raises her hands to cover her face.
Pexels / Ksenia Chernaya

MANILA, Philippines — Eighty percent of Filipino children have experienced some form of violence at home, school, workplace, community or in dating relationships, the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines (CEAP) revealed as it called for stronger child protection measures in Catholic schools through a protocol.

“The CANE+D Protocol, covering Child Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation and Discrimination, should be a serious concern for Catholic education because the scale of violence against children in the Philippines tells us that child protection cannot remain at the level of policy statements,” CEAP said.

The association noted that aside from the 4th National Plan of Action for Children report, the United Nations Children’s Fund reported that three in five children experienced violent discipline, about one in three experienced school bullying and one in five children who use the internet have experienced sexual abuse or exploitation online.

In 2023 alone, the Philippine National Police Women and Children Protection Center received 18,756 reports of child rights violations, of which 17,304 involved violence against children, including child abuse, rape and acts of lasciviousness.

“These figures remind us that a school may be one of the places where a child first discloses harm or where warning signs are first seen. The revised CANE+D protocol therefore matters because it establishes a more coordinated pathway for identification, reporting, investigation, case management, legal proceedings, rehabilitation, reintegration and prevention,” CEAP added.
CEAP said the protocol brings teachers and other frontline workers into the protection system and calls for specialized training for personnel handling CANE+D cases.

The Department of the Interior and Local Government has directed local government units to adopt and implement the revised CANE+D Protocol and strengthen coordinated referral and case-management systems involving social workers, law enforcement, health professionals, educators and other frontline actors, CEAP said.

“For Catholic schools, this is ultimately a question of mission: when the dignity of a child is wounded, how prepared are we to recognize it, respond to it, protect the child and walk with the child toward healing?” it asked.

“Healing, therefore, cannot mean simply helping a child feel better after something has happened. In Catholic education, healing must include protection, truth, accountability, accompaniment, restoration, and the rebuilding of trust,” CEAP said.

SINGAPORE – Malacañang has called for a deeper probe into the claims of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte and members of her family on the instructions of former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Palace press officer Claire Castro said evidence would show who is credible among those making conflicting claims.
She said Gracioso has shown that he was with the Vice President in some “personal” events.

“The investigation on this should be deeper, not for anyone but for the people because this involves public funds. Even if they claim that this is just politicking and that is their sole defense, those who are investigating this should not be stopped,” Castro said at a press briefing here.?
Duterte has denied Gracioso’s claims, saying the former policeman’s statements may have been motivated by money.
Velasco’s camp refuted the accusation, dismissing it as a “one-size-fits-all” narration “designed and fabricated to attack as many targets as it can while being inconsistent with verifiable events.”
Meanwhile, Duterte’s camp lashed back at Castro over the latter’s statement that the Vice President knows alleged bagmen Ramil Madriaga and Gracioso.
“No one prevents anybody from playing dumb. But it’s embarrassing,” defense spokesman Michael Poa said. - Bella Cariaso

articles.title: COA upholds disallowance of P73.29 million OVP secret funds
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit has affirmed with finality the disallowance against the Office of the Vice President (OVP)’s P73.29 million in confidential funds that were spent in just 11 days in…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am
The photo of the Commission on Audit's office in Quezon City.
The STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Audit has affirmed with finality the disallowance against the Office of the Vice President (OVP)’s P73.29 million in confidential funds that were spent in just 11 days in December 2022.

In a 15-page decision dated Oct. 5, the COA denied for lack of merit the motion for reconsideration filed by Vice President Sara Duterte, special disbursing officer Gina Acosta and OVP chief accountant Julieta Villadelrey.
It upheld its April 10 ruling that affirmed the notice of disallowance issued by the COA Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office on Aug. 8, 2024.
“The office has already anticipated the possibility of this decision and has prepared to respond through the appropriate legal and institutional channels,” the OVP said.
The OVP, however, said it has yet to receive a copy of the Oct. 5 COA resolution.
The notice covered expenses made from Dec. 21 to 31, 2022, from the total of P125-million confidential funds that the OVP received on Dec. 20 that year.
The disallowed amount included P69.787 million in rewards and P3.5 million in payments for tables, chairs, desktop computers and printers.
According to the notice, rewards were paid out as P10 million in cash, P34.857 million in various goods and P24.93 million in medicines.

The COA pointed out that the notice of disallowance was issued due to the failure of the OVP to submit documents showing the success of information-gathering and/or surveillance activities to support the payments of rewards to informers, as required by Joint Circular No. 2015-01 or the guidelines on the use of confidential and intelligence funds.
Instead, the COA said the OVP submitted a list of activities that the Vice President and officers of OVP satellite offices attended from Dec. 13 to 31, 2022.
Moreover, the list did not indicate or narrate the accomplishments that resulted from the information gathered or in the surveillance activities.
It also did not give weight to the OVP’s argument that the absence of untoward security-related incidents showed that it had complied with the requirement, saying such “does not hold water.”

The audit body also pointed out that the OVP submitted a certification from the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSG) listing routine security activities such as casing, liaising, surveillance, profiling and ocular inspections.

But the VPSG, as salaried personnel of the AFP, are “fundamentally disqualified” from receiving informer rewards under the joint circular, the COA said, and that submitting acknowledgement receipts for payments to salaried personnel, without proof of operational success from eligible non-employee informers, rendered the P69.787 million “completely unsubstantiated and disallowable in audit.” – Bella Cariaso

MANILA, Philippines — The House of Representatives has approved on second reading the government’s proposed P7.2-trillion spending plan for fiscal year 2027.
Third reading approval is expected to be on Oct. 12 after House leaders requested the Senate’s permission to extend their legislative calendar to pass the budget bill on final reading.

The floor adopted amendments reallocating around P116 billion from the National Expenditure Program, following recommendations from a select committee of ranking lawmakers to augment flagship state assistance projects and infrastructure.

MANILA, Philippines — The country is expected to import more than five million metric tons (MT) of rice this year to strengthen supply as domestic production is projected to decline due to the effects of El Niño, according to the Department of Agriculture.
The Philippines has imported 3.98 million MT of rice as of Sept. 24, which has already surpassed last year’s 3.39 million MT.
Among the top sources of rice was Vietnam at 2.72 million MT, followed by Thailand at 517,528 MT and Myanmar at 400,359 MT.
