articles.title: What's the fire danger from lithium batteries?
articles.summary: Firefighters have raised alarms about hot, fast, hard-to-extinguish fires in lithium batteries from e-bikes in people's homes and huge storage batteries at a P.E.I. solar farm. Here's why lithium…

image.caption: A 2024 e-bike fire in a Toronto subway car led to a seasonal e-bike transit ban. Lithium batteries, especially from e-bikes, are a growing cause of fires across Canada.

blocks.text: Firefighters have raised alarms about hot, fast, hard-to-extinguish fires in lithium batteries from e-bikes in people's homes (including one in Toronto just this week) and huge storage batteries at a P.E.I. solar farm last month.

Concerns about lithium battery fires have led to bans of electric bikes and cars in some buildings, public transit and ferries, causing problems for people who rely on them. They've also made some people hesitant about trying electric vehicles.
This week is Fire Prevention Week, and lithium batteries are the official theme. Here's a closer look at why lithium battery fires are a challenge and what can be done to minimize the risks.
Why lithium-ion batteries are so dangerous
How common are lithium battery fires?

Canadian fire departments don't track them in a consistent way, but a survey from the Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs estimates there were 1,500 fires started by lithium batteries in 600 communities across the country last year. Their numbers are growing exponentially with the numbers of lithium battery-powered devices, says Paul Boissoneault, president of the association and chief of the Oakville Fire Department.
Lithium battery fires are most common for devices found in people's homes, especially e-bikes and e-scooters.

EV and energy storage batteries are far rarer, as they're rigorously tested and have built-in safety features like temperature sensors and systems that cool battery cells as needed. Canada-wide statistics on EV fires aren't available, although U.S. data suggests they're extremely uncommon compared to fires in gas-powered vehicles.
LISTEN | Separating fact from fiction about EV battery fires:
What On Earth28:30Separating fact from fiction about EV battery fires
Grid storage battery fires are even less common — a global database from the Electric Power Research Institute shows the one in P.E.I. was one of only six worldwide this year.

items: As Summerside works to contain fire at solar farm, this expert says such fires are rare

blocks.text: What causes lithium battery fires?
Batteries rely on the separation of their positive and negative terminals. That forces electrons to move through the device you're powering to get from one end of the battery to the other.

A barrier material keeps the terminals separated. When a hole (effectively a short circuit) forms in that barrier, fire happens, said Randy Narine, a professional firefighter in Brampton, Ont., who studies lithium battery safety through his company Clean Core Research, in an interview with CBC's What on Earth?
That hole can be caused by wear and tear over time or from damage, such as a collision or someone dropping a battery from a smaller device, such as an e-bike.

Lithium battery fires can also be started from overheating — due to overcharging or improper charging (such as with the wrong charger) or heat exposure from an external heat source, including a fire in a nearby battery cell in the same battery, since many batteries contain multiple cells.
Regina fire chief gives reminder to check charging devices
What makes them dangerous compared to other fires?

They can burn "hotter and faster" than other fires, Boissoneault said. At a certain temperature, lithium batteries reach "thermal runaway," where heat triggers and speeds up chemical reactions in the battery that generate more heat.
This can lead to a "massive chain reaction" and a potentially explosive fire, Narine said.

They make their own oxygen. One of the battery's terminals is made of a metal oxide that breaks down into metal and oxygen gas during a fire, further sustaining the fire. That means normal techniques to smother fires don't work.

They generate toxic substances such as hydrogen fluoride as materials in the battery break down in the heat. They can also contaminate firefighters' clothing and equipment with toxic compounds such as formaldehyde and heavy metals that need to be removed afterward.

They can reignite hours, days or weeks later, thanks to thermal runaway and their oxygen self-generation. Boissoneault said that can have implications for how the burned batteries are transported and stored after a fire.
The fire at this P.E.I. solar farm is finally out. Officials warn it could reignite

Firefighters don't always feel prepared for them. Boissoneault said just 40 per cent of departments surveyed had formal training on dealing with lithium battery incidents, and even fewer said they had standard operating policies and the correct equipment to deal with such emergencies. Many also don't have a way to decontaminate their gear after a lithium fire.
How can they be handled and extinguished?

EV fires are typically sprayed with huge amounts of water. Narine estimated a gas car fire can be extinguished with less than 2,000 litres of water, whereas it can take tens of thousands of litres to put out a lithium battery fire.
While water can provide cooling and can sometimes be used to protect nearby materials from catching fire, it can't actually smother the battery fire.
Why has a battery been burning for nearly 2 weeks at Summerside's solar farm?
In many cases, fire experts say, the fire just needs to burn out.
That's particularly the case for large energy storage batteries, said experts at a fire safety panel at the Energy Storage Canada conference in Toronto in September.

Adam Jakubowski, a firefighter and senior consultant with Energy Safety Response Group specializing in battery energy storage systems, said in many cases, putting water on a lithium battery fire simply prolongs a fire, which may reignite a week or month later. It can also lead to water runoff that could contaminate the environment.
Toronto's fire chief calls e-bike batteries the 'greatest public fire safety risk'
What can you do to reduce the risk?
Buy batteries with certification labels such as CSA, cUL or CETL rather than cheaper ones that may not have safety features. Don't modify batteries to charge more quickly or hold more charge.

Charge devices properly, on hard surfaces, away from any combustible materials, and unplug as soon as they're fully charged, Boissoneault says. Charge with the right charger for that device. "Don't mix and match," says Jon McQuaid, vice-president of marketing communications and safety for Call2Recycle Canada, a non-profit focused on battery collection and recycling.

Recycle them only at battery-recycling dropoff sites, not trash or regular recycling bins, McQuaid said. He advises taping over the terminals (even for tiny button batteries) first to protect from debris or other batteries that could cause a spark, "which could then lead to a thermal runaway."
Damaged batteries need to be placed in special "damaged, defective or recalled" battery containers at select battery dropoff sites.
What can you do to prevent a lithium-ion battery fire in your home?

articles.title: Gaza is slowly moving beyond survival mode — 3 years after the war began
articles.summary: As Israelis and Palestinians mark the sombre anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack that began the three-year war between Israel and Hamas, people in Gaza are also starting to look to the future.…

image.caption: Mohammed Barghout looks at produce at the Gaza City market late last month. Three years after the war began, there are now more food options available in the strip, but much of it remains unaffordable to average Palestinians. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

blocks.text: The roads in Gaza are still littered with rubble, garbage and the ruins of lopsided buildings. But three years into the Israel-Hamas war and almost a year into the fragile ceasefire, the airstrikes, bombs and wails of people calling for loved ones have faded. Now, the air is filled with distant chatter, cars honking and the sounds of life.

On Wednesday, Israelis and Palestinians will mark the sombre anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, that claimed the lives of 1,200 people, with 251 hostages in Gaza, according to Israeli tallies. The war has left some 74,245 people dead in Gaza, according to the local health ministry. Since the Oct. 11 ceasefire last year, the ministry says 1,462 Palestinians have been killed.

Today, the enclave is slowly moving beyond survival mode as many civilians begin to think about the future, looking for viable longer-term housing and considering sending kids back to school. CBC News spoke with six people in Gaza to ask them how they’re managing with shelter, food and education.

items: Israeli strikes kill 5, including 4 women, in Gaza, health officials say
Palestinian death toll in Gaza war rises above 74,000 since war began

blocks.text: Shelter still at a premium

Throughout the war, Gazans were constantly displaced and many camps popped up throughout the enclave as people sought safe spaces. Since the ceasefire, these displacements have become less frequent and many are now considering where to set up more permanent lodgings.

Mohamed Al-Arabeed, 44, and his family of eight have been living at the Al-Maqousi camp near Gaza City for three years. But the tent that cost him 2,000 shekels (about $935 Cdn) is now falling apart at the seams.

Mohamed Al-Arabeed lives with his family in the Al-Maqousi camp near Gaza City. He says he's been patching up his tent and trying to keep it together after it went through three winters in Gaza. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)
"We’re piling nylon on it to get through the winter,” he told CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife earlier this month.
Gaza City is near the yellow line signifying the edge of Israeli military control in the strip. Al-Arabeed says people are still scared to run errands in case they get caught in fighting or a strike.
"We don't know how long we will stay like this," he said. "We are not guilty of what happened or what might happen."

In another part of Gaza City, Abdullah Abu Hajar, 47, lives in a partially collapsed building with his family of eight. Red spray paint marking the building reads, in Arabic, "dangerous, could collapse."

Officials in Gaza City used red spray paint to mark the building where Abdullah Abu Hajar and his family live as 'dangerous, could collapse.' He says the 17 families living in the building say they have nowhere else to go. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)
The walls are still standing but some of the floors are tilted and fold together like an accordion.
Abu Hajar told CBC News last week that the 17 families living there all feel they have nowhere else to go.

items: At least 21 killed in Gaza, including many children, as unstable building collapses

blocks.text: "I'm scared, I don't sleep. I stay up all night to check on people in the building."
He says it shakes sometimes, and when it gets very bad, he and others call on their wives and children to prepare to leave.
They died in 2023. They were only buried last week
Food options limited, pricey

In August 2025, a global hunger monitor reported that famine conditions existed in Gaza City. It was the first official confirmation of famine after months of warnings by aid groups that the war and Israel's border restrictions were causing starvation among Palestinians, particularly children.

In December 2024, when Mohammed Barghout, took CBC News to Gaza City's market, he found steep prices for the little food available and spent 200 shekels (about $93 Cdn) on just a plate of cooked rice and some diapers.
When the 49-year-old father of four returned for a shopping trip last month, he saw eggplants, potatoes and tomatoes. He says while there may be more options, they're still not very affordable.
"I don't see many people," Barghout said. "Maybe they don't have money to buy things."

Barghout looks at eggs at the Gaza City market late last month. Currently, two dozen eggs costs 30 shekels, or about $14 Cdn. The father of four says it would cost about 500 shekels ($234 Cdn) to feed his family breakfast, and that's something he can't afford. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)
Today, two dozen eggs cost 30 shekels, or about $14 Cdn, while one potato is five shekels, about $2.35 Cdn.
While he visits many stalls to ask for prices, Barghout often leaves without buying. "I want to buy mangoes for my children, but I cannot afford it, so I will wait."
He leaves with just three potatoes for his whole family.

items: In Gaza, a UN cash-for-work program gives Palestinians some income — and hope
Gaza has become frozen in 'humanitarian purgatory' — and it could get worse

blocks.text: Many in Gaza don’t bother with the market at all.

Late last month, Ola Al-Masri was using the flour she received from an aid package to bake bread on an open flame. She and her husband live in Khan Younis with their three children in the ruins of Al-Aqsa University.
The Al-Masris still rely heavily on food distribution points set up by Palestinians who cook soups and stews in batches and hand them out to those in need.
A boy reaches out with a bucket in hand at a food distribution centre west of Khan Younis in Gaza in November 2024. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)
Images of people crowding these distribution points — piling on top of each other, waving pots and screaming for their portions — became synonymous with the struggle for food during the war.
Things look much the same today.

Ola is first in line at the fence as a crowd gathers. She waves her pot until she gets the attention of a volunteer who doles out a portion of the day's meal, a soup that will be lunch and dinner for her family. After securing one portion, she rejoins the line, hoping she might get more.
"This is my routine every day," she said. "I wait here for two or three hours, waiting for food."
Israel marks 3 years since Oct. 7 attacks as Palestinians mourn Gaza's destruction
Education a priority again
Back in Gaza City, Rasha Al-Dos, 44, gets her four children ready for school at the parking garage she converted into rooms using tarps and wood.
This morning, she sends her youngest son, four-year-old Munzer, to his nearby kindergarten class before getting ready for school herself.
After losing her husband during the war, Al-Dos returned to her work as a teacher at Warda al-Huda private school, about a 10-minute bus ride away.

Rasha Al-Dos teaches students in her classroom at Warda Al-Huda, a private school in Gaza City last month. She returned to teaching to support her four children after her husband died during the war. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

Though many buildings in Gaza were reduced to rubble, her school didn't suffer as much damage. Al-Dos’s classroom is mostly intact, but for one blown-out wall that's covered by a white tarp painted with the English and Arabic alphabet.
Al-Dos says about a quarter of the students she taught before the war did not survive.

items: They're strapped for supplies, and danger looms. But Gaza’s children are thrilled to be back in school
In war-torn Gaza, students strive to study and professors are compelled to teach

blocks.text: Her students today are lucky, she says, as many can’t afford to return to traditional school and instead attend informal classes in tents.
After three years with no education at all, she's just grateful to be teaching again.
"Alhamdulillah, we have the power and the strength to … go on and teach our children."

articles.title: Immigration minister appears unaware of court ruling that guarantees Charter rights for refugees
articles.summary: Refugee rights advocates say they are shocked to hear that the federal immigration minister appeared in an interview with Radio-Canada to be unfamiliar with the landmark Supreme Court decision widely…

image.caption: In an interview with Radio-Canada, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab was repeatedly asked about the landmark 1985 Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration decision. She appeared to be unfamiliar with the case. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Refugee rights advocates say they are shocked to hear that the federal immigration minister appeared in an interview with Radio-Canada to be unfamiliar with the landmark Supreme Court decision widely considered to be the cornerstone of the Canadian refugee protection system.
Supreme Court's landmark Singh decision led to establishment of Refugee Board

Refugee rights advocates say they are shocked that the federal immigration minister appeared to be unfamiliar with the landmark Supreme Court decision widely considered to be the cornerstone of the Canadian refugee protection system.
In an interview with Radio-Canada, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab was repeatedly asked about the 1985 Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration case.
This Singh decision ruled that asylum seekers are guaranteed the Charter right to fundamental justice and led to the creation of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada.
It is also a key argument in the legal challenge to the Carney government's immigration reforms that restrict who is eligible for Refugee Board hearings.

items: 'You are a very bad minister,' immigration critic says at tense meeting
Canadians born abroad caught up in citizenship certificate delays

blocks.text: "Honestly, I was extremely shocked," said Gauri Sreenivasan, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees. "It's very concerning that the minister in charge of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada would not be fully aware of the Supreme Court's Singh decision."
Diab was interviewed in July by Radio-Canada's Les murs: le périple des migrants vers le Canada, a documentary podcast launched three weeks ago that examines Canada's asylum system.
She was asked a series of questions, including about the Safe Third Country Agreement and Bill C-12, the Carney government's immigration reforms passed last March.

One of the most controversial changes in C-12 was that asylum claims made more than a year after an individual's first entry into Canada are no longer referred to the Refugee Board, but instead are given a pre-removal risk assessment.

The assessment is conducted by an Immigration Canada officer to ensure that a person is not at risk of being tortured or killed if returned to their country — and typically includes a written submission rather than an oral hearing.
Migrant rights rally calls on government to change immigration policy
Diab said in French that Bill C-12 "respects our Canadian Charter," adding that she herself is a lawyer and that the changes are meant to address the backlog in asylum cases.

When pressed about the argument that under the Singh decision asylum seekers have a constitutional right to an oral hearing, she replied that since the law is new, the government would continue to monitor the situation.
Radio-Canada then asked her point-blank if she was familiar with the Singh decision. After a pause, Diab asked that the name of the decision be repeated.
When told again that it was the Singh decision handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1985, she said she would have to check with her team.
"There are many Singhs and many decisions," said Diab.
Immigration minister asked about court ruling that guarantees Charter rights for refugees
Radio-Canada then specified that it was the decision that led to the creation of the Refugee Board, to which she responded: "Ah, OK."
With the Singh decision, the Supreme Court of Canada recognized, among other things, the right of asylum seekers to an oral hearing, according to several experts Radio-Canada spoke with.

"[The claimant] is entitled to a full hearing on their file so that they can explain their situation before a competent decision-maker," said François Crépeau, professor emeritus of public international law at McGill University and former United Nations special rapporteur on the human rights of migrants.
"That is why the Immigration and Refugee Board was created in 1989. It was to meet the requirements of the Singh decision."
Bill C-12 is being challenged in the courts. Lawyers allege it violates Canada's legal obligations under both domestic and international law.

items: Canada's new asylum law puts Iranians in limbo
Where is Canada's immigration minister? Community groups are asking

blocks.text: Immigration Canada maintains that the Singh decision is respected by Bill C-12.

"The Supreme Court in Singh found that in order to meet the requirements of fundamental justice, an oral hearing is required when there is a credibility issue at stake. The Supreme Court did not find that in all cases an oral hearing is required," a department lawyer told a parliamentary committee studying Bill C-12 in February.
Crépeau disagrees: "Removing a full hearing … is a violation of the conditions set by the Singh decision."
Immediately after the interview, Diab's office insisted that the minister was well aware of the Singh decision, but that due to the language barrier she had not fully understood the questions.
The podcast interview was conducted in French, which is not Diab's first language.

However, during two appearances in English before two different Senate committees studying Bill C-12, the minister also did not answer questions regarding the Singh decision, deferring to department officials and lawyers.
'Issue of competence': advocate
"I believe there is certainly an issue of competence," said Louis-Philippe Jannard of TCRI, a Quebec umbrella association of more than 160 organizations working with refugees and immigrants.

"The issue of the Singh decision was raised during the legislative process for Bill C-12 before both the House of Commons and the Senate. So for it not to be on the minister's radar is surprising to say the least."
Radio-Canada asked the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) whether, given these criticisms, Diab still has the confidence of Prime Minister Mark Carney.

PMO spokesperson Renée LeBlanc Proctor said in an email to Radio-Canada that Diab plays an "essential" role in the implementation of the federal government's mandate to bring down immigration to "viable" levels while attracting the best talent in the world.
"She continues this work," Proctor said.

Diab was previously criticized by immigrant rights groups who said the minister was hard to reach and did not seem to have a firm grasp of her cabinet portfolio. The Opposition Conservatives have been calling for Diab to be fired for months.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Brigitte Bureau is an award-winning investigative reporter with Radio-Canada. You can reach her by email: brigitte.bureau@radio-canada.ca.

articles.title: Family of Hamilton-born hockey player Matthew Mayich says new university review into his collapse falls short
articles.summary: Arizona State University says it commissioned an independent review to make recommendations following the collapse and hospitalization of Canadian NHL prospect Matthew Mayich during a workout.…

image.caption: Hamilton-born Matthew Mayich, who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed. (St. Louis Blues)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Arizona State University says it commissioned an independent review to make recommendations following the collapse and hospitalization of Canadian NHL prospect Matthew Mayich during a workout. Mayich's family lawyer says the review falls short because it's focused on policy rather than accountability.
Mayich remains hospitalized after he collapsed during a workout at Arizona State University

Arizona State University, where Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapsed during a workout on a hot August day, says it commissioned an independent review to make recommendations on how to safely train athletes outdoors and how to respond to "adverse events or reactions."
A lawyer representing the family of 21-year-old Mayich says the review is "not what's needed right now," because it won't address who is responsible for what happened to the student hockey player.

In a separate review published in September, Arizona State University (ASU) official James Rund wrote Mayich collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during Aug. 20 training at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus. It also determined school hockey coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.

Mayich remains in hospital. His parents, Christina and John Mayich, previously told CBC News he's "a fighter" and they're not giving up on him. The family's lawyers at U..S. firm Hagens Berman have told CBC the 21-year-old suffered heatstroke and "needs a miracle."

items: Arizona university hockey coach put on paid leave after report on Canadian player Matthew Mayich's collapse

blocks.text: Mayich's family and teammates raised questions and concerns
On Oct. 2, Jay Thorne, ASU's vice-president of media relations shared a communication from Rund — ASU senior vice-present — to university present Michael Crow.

In it, Rund said ASU retained former Supreme Court of Arizona Chief Justice Scott Bales to lead "an independent review of the facts that have been identified by the university, attorneys for the Mayich family, attorneys for members of the ASU hockey team, law enforcement agencies, and others as appropriate."

The Mayich family and their attorneys have questioned the circumstances of the Aug. 20 workout and how coaches and school officials responded to the player's collapse. Mayich's parents say their son — who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023 — was healthy prior to the workout. Lawyers have said the "military-style," session took place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.

In a Sept. 28 anonymous letter to Crow, some of Mayich's ASU Sun Devils teammates alleged Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout and called for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.
Two days later, the school put ASU hockey coach Greg Powers on paid administrative leave.
Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout
According to Rund's Oct. 2 letter, the new independent review by Bales will result in recommendations for:

items: Planning and approving outdoor athletic activities.
Staffing, policies and procedures for outdoor athletics, including "adjustments necessary to address changing conditions or adverse reactions."
Preparing for and responding to "adverse events or reactions" occurring during outdoor athletics.
Using outside consultants for planning and delivering "strength and conditioning and practice activities."

blocks.text: Student athletes at ASU will be invited to participate in the review with confidential and anonymous options, Rund said.
ASU requested Bales's review be completed by early December, Rund added.

"Justice Bales is a respected choice, and he will do an excellent job," lawyer Rob Carey said in an Oct. 2 statement to reporters on behalf of the Mayich family. "But ASU hired him to review policies that may help prevent a tragedy like this in the future."

items: Matthew Mayich's Arizona teammates dispute school report on workout before Hamilton NHL prospect's collapse

blocks.text: Investigation not set up to answer key questions: lawyer

"What is necessary, and what the Mayich family has asked for and deserves, is an investigation of what went wrong on that field and who is responsible," Carey said. "Justice Bales has not been asked to answer those fundamental questions."
Carey said ASU needs to answer how the workout happened, why it didn't stop when players were in "visible distress" and which ASU and athletics association rules were broken.

The university, Carey said, should "expand Justice Bales's mandate to cover the questions that matter and let him bring in the expertise he needs," or, it should have a second independent investigation into the actions of ASU employees.
He added Bales's findings should be made public and until "the work is done," ASU should keep coaches who were involved away from players.
ASU said Sept. 30 that it appointed assistant coach Mike Corbett to lead the hockey team after it put Powers on leave.

items: Hockey coaches didn't submit training plan before Matthew Mayich collapsed in workout: Arizona university

blocks.text: CBC Hamilton asked ASU to respond to the family's concerns. The university did not respond prior to publication.

In an Oct. 5 news release, Arizona State Legislature House and Senate education chairs Matt Gress and Hildy Angius said they welcome Bales's review, noting they had called for an independent investigation.
Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 then with the Ottawa 67's before the St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Justin Chandler is a CBC News reporter in Hamilton. He covers stories of all kinds from places including picket lines, court rooms, council meetings and research labs. Justin has a special interest in how public policy affects people, and loves a quirky human-interest story. Before CBC Hamilton, he worked for TVO and on a variety of CBC teams and programs. He co-hosted Radio Free Krypton on Met Radio.

articles.summary:
Ukraine president confirms series of attacks on Pryluky, Dnipro, Kremenchik, Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched “one fo the most vile…

blocks.text: At least 11 dead, 34 injured after 'vile' attack on Ukraine on Putin's birthday, Zelenskyy says

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched “one fo the most vile strikes” on Ukraine last night, targeting the country’s energy infrastructure overnight.

At least 11 people were killed, and more than 34 injured in a series of attacks on Pryluky, Dnipro, Kremenchik, Zaporizhzhia, and Kyiv, which Zelenskyy ironically called “a birthday gift for Putin” who turns 74 today.

blocks.caption: Rescuers work at a site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian missile strike in the town of Pryluky, Chernihiv region, Ukraine. Photograph: State Emergency Service Of Ukraine/Reuters

blocks.text: “Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity. That is why every day we are looking for missiles for Patriot systems that can and must actually protect people’s lives here, in Ukrainian skies,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha went further, saying:
“On Putin’s birthday, Russian generals brought him his favorite present: war crimes.”
He added:

“What Russian generals fail to tell Putin is that he is not winning this war and never will. … I urge all partners to give Putin real presents that will help him finally choose diplomacy over war. Stronger sanctions on his military-industrial complex, including facilities producing ballistic missiles and the Rassvet satellite system, as well as stronger support for Ukraine, including all kinds of air defense and energy assistance ahead of winter. But his ultimate present will be a dock in The Hague. We are preparing the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine for practical launch already next year. Putin and his friends should know that accountability is inevitable.”

Elsewhere, I will bring you the latest from France, as high school protests continue after a major march in Paris, which ended with sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, and officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.

Following allegations of police brutality, interior minister Laurent Nuñez suspended the use of stun grenades at the protests, after a 15-year-old reportedly lost a hand on Monday, and a 14-year old lost several teeth.
The French PM, Sébastien Lecornu, is expected to speak later today to set out his plans for responding to the protests.
I will bring you also all other news from across Europe.
It’s Wednesday, 7 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Emerging economies are embracing solar power and skipping fossil fuels much faster than Europe or the US
articles.summary: Renewable electricity is cheaper than ever. While the West got rich on coal and oil, some of the world's poorest countries are banking on solar, wind and water instead.

image.caption: Solar panels are becoming a common sight in rural parts of Ethiopia. Farmers who previously used diesel generators for irrigation are switching to solar power, like here in the village Dore Bafeno in the Sidama region in 2026.Image: Shewangizaw Wegayehu/DW

blocks.text: As emerging economies and global living standards rise, is the world in for another fossil fuel boom? The data says not. Countries from Southeast Asia to Sub-Saharan Africa aren't investing in fossil fuels as the West did; they're investing in electricity powered by renewables.

When the US and Europe industrialized in the 19th and 20th centuries, they did so using fossil energy. From coal ovens, gas heating and combustion-engine cars to electricity produced in coal and gas power plants, entire societies relied on polluting fuels.
Yet while burning fossil fuels allowed industrialized countries to boom, it also caused the climate crisis that is linked to extreme weather events around the world today.
Renewable electricity is rapidly becoming the cheapest option
Many of the same countries that became economically powerful off the back of fossil fuels are now trying to transition to renewables, but centuries of legacy infrastructure hold them back.

Because a gas boiler won't run on wind power and a diesel truck cannot be solar-powered, societies looking to shift to green energy need to use more electricity and increase their share of renewables.

That is where many middle- and lower-income countries have an advantage. With less existing energy infrastructure built around fossil fuels, they are better placed for a faster rollout of renewable electricity sources.

In many instances, solar power in particular is now cheaper to produce than fossil electricity. And unlike large coal or gas plants, which take years to construct and millions in investments, solar and wind farms can be built quickly and with much less upfront cost.

At the same time, according to an analysis by renewables think tank Ember, electronic devices like refrigerators, electric stoves or air conditioners have all become much cheaper in the last decades, making electricity a more affordable option as an energy source for cooking, heating and more.

While electric cars are still a luxury item in most places, their prices are coming down too. And a UN study found that in India, Indonesia and Vietnam electric scooters and motorbikes already cost the same as petrol models. Yet a lot less to fuel.
All this means that renewable electricity is quickly becoming the best choice for the wallet — not just for the climate. And countries are taking note.

"We're seeing a leapfrog take place right across the emerging markets,” said Kingsmill Bond, energy strategist at Ember. "The whole of Asia is electrifying quickly, and the whole of Europe and the United States is stagnant."
Lower-income countries are electrifying faster
In 2023, only around a quarter of global electricity was generated by renewables. But that figure is rising fast, and almost all new capacity added these days is based on solar or wind power.
Lower-income countries already use less fossil fuels and more renewables than higher-income ones.

And large middle-income economies are outpacing richer ones as well. In 2023, solar power alone made up at least six percent and ten percent of electricity in India and Vietnam, respectively. The global average was five percent.
Lower-income countries are electrifying without the fossil detour

This boom has meant middle- and lower-income countries are electrifying fast, consuming less energy directly from fossil fuels than richer countries. Vietnam, for instance, is already using more electricity than the US, Europe and even China, and India is following the same path.
But the potential for energy leapfrogging might be particularly high in low-income countries, especially across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia and Namibia are rapidly expanding their energy infrastructure to meet the demands of a growing, young population. But rural areas in many countries are not connected to electricity grids.
Joel Nana, project manager at South African NGO Sustainable Energy Africa says that "even when there is access to power, it's often not reliable."

Until a few years ago, he says, people defaulted to diesel generators to meet their energy needs. That came at a cost because importing fuel is particularly expensive in many African countries, meaning energy crises and oil price fluctuations hit much harder.
Renewables for energy access and independence
These factors make solar power a solution for both energy access and independence. And it has become so cheap that Nana says it's a "no-brainer."

"Some businesses can make back their investment in just two years, so why would you want to deploy anything else?” he said. "Solar has rapidly become the de facto default technology that everyone falls back on.”

And once it is set up, it is very effective. Sub-Saharan Africa is extremely well-suited to solar power. It gets more sun than almost anywhere in the world, and has enough space for solar farms to cover electricity demand hundreds of times over.
"If you add solar plus batteries, you can get cheap electricity about 90 percent of the time from the sun alone”, said Kingsmill Bond.
Countries like Namibia, South Africa, Kenya and Senegal have expanded their solar capacity massively in the past few years.

In a 2026 report for African Tech Futures Lab and Ember, Nana analyzed import data from China and estimated that around 100,000 solar panels were installed across Africa every day in 2026, up 45 percent from just the previous year.

Similar trends are emerging all across the world. In Pakistan, for example, people have been buying solar panels from China en masse in the past few years to avoid steep electricity grid prices and frequent power outages.
Cheap energy boosts economies

Aleksi Lumijärvi, director for knowledge, policy and finance at the International Renewable Energy Association says these decisions can have a major impact on the global economy in the coming decades.
"Industrial companies will find that it will be cheaper to move production to, for example, somewhere in Sub-Saharan Africa, because they have this cheap, clean solar power plus batteries available.”
Kingsmill Bond says where electricity is cheap and abundant, wealth will follow.
"You're going to have faster growth in the emerging markets, you will have fewer financial crises. It will make a material difference to people's quality of lives.”
Nana says the next step for African countries is to establish policies that ensure everyone benefits from the solar boom.

"We are heading towards the most decentralized grid in the whole world within the next five years,” he told DW. His mantra for governments, he says, is: "This is happening, whether you like it or not.” He expects a wave of new energy regulations, many of which are now in the final stages of negotiation, to come into effect across Africa in the coming months and years.
"Countries are realizing it's in their interest to integrate this technology into national strategies, to share the benefits and to make use of this competitive advantage."
All data and code behind this analysis can be found in this Github repository.
More data-driven stories by DW can be found here.

articles.title: Oscar-winning actress Eva Marie Saint dies aged 102
articles.summary: She starred opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, then alongside Cary Grant in Hitchcock's North by Northwest.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Eve Marie Saint has two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame
ByPaul Glynn
Culture reporter
Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar-winning actress who starred in Hollywood classics such as On the Waterfront and North by Northwest, has died aged 102.

Saint won the Academy Award for best supporting actress for her movie debut in director Elia Kazan's 1954 crime drama On the Waterfront, playing Edie Doyle, the love interest of Marlon Brando's conflicted boxer-turned-docker.
Five years later, she portrayed femme fatale Eve Kendall, dangerously seducing Cary Grant's entangled advertising executive in Alfred Hitchcock's spy thriller, North by Northwest.
She died on Tuesday of natural causes, surrounded by family and loved ones at her home in Los Angeles, family representative Jeff Sanderson confirmed.
Until her death, Saint was the oldest surviving Oscar winner and one of the last remaining stars of Hollywood's golden age.
She also won an Emmy in 1990 for her role as a rich widow in the acclaimed TV miniseries People Like Us.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The star pictured in around 1960

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The star pictured in around 1960

blocks.caption: Image caption, Saint alongside Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront

blocks.text: Image source, 20th Century-Fox/Getty Images
Saint alongside Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront
Born in Newark, New Jersey in 1924, Saint had originally intended to become a teacher before developing a passion for theatre.
She trained in New York at the Herbert Berghof Studio and then the Actors Studio - the home of method acting - co-founded by Kazan.
Saint burst on to the Hollywood scene with her performance in Kazan's classic, On the Waterfront.
Brando was known as an intense method actor and Saint admitted to having found him "adorable" but "a little frightening".
"I felt that he could see right through me," she told Turner Classic Movies (TCM) in a 2013 interview.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The actress opposite Cary Grant in North by Northwest (above and below)

blocks.text: Image source, Photo by 20th Century-Fox/Getty Images
The actress opposite Cary Grant in North by Northwest (above and below)

blocks.caption: Cary Grant holding Eva Marie Saint in a scene from the film 'North By Northwest', 1959

blocks.text: She was considered a surprise choice, though, to play one of "Hitchcock's blondes", as they were known at the time, in his masterpiece North by Northwest.
Her co-star Grant was known for being very demanding of his leading ladies.
"He worked with me from the outside in," said Saint.
"My hair, my makeup, my shoes, my jewellery, my purse, my gloves, everything. And just from creating that exterior for me, he gave me the sense of a spy lady."
Saint also starred opposite Paul Newman in Otto Preminger's Exodus in 1960, and she was Warren Beatty's love interest in John Frankenheimer's All Fall Down.
But she then stepped away from the limelight to raise a family with director Jeffrey Hayden.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Eva Marie Saint (centre) pictured with co-stars for the 2006 premiere of Superman Returns in California

blocks.text: Eva Marie Saint (centre) pictured with co-stars for the 2006 premiere of Superman Returns in California
Half a century later, Saint - by then in her early 80s - made a big screen comeback as Superman's adoptive mother in the 2006 blockbuster Superman Returns.
And she later had parts in the supernatural fantasy Winter's Tale, alongside Colin Farrell and Russell Crowe, and another in the 2019 nun drama Mariette in Ecstasy.
Saint, who has two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, said her longevity in acting had given her work extra depth.
"The longer you live, the smarter you get, because you've been around, you've seen things," she told TCM.
"You've gone through different emotional experiences in your own life, and hopefully, you understand things better.
"And that makes you a better actress."
Saint's marriage to Hayden lasted for 65 years, until his death in 2016, and she is survived by their two children.

articles.title: ‘Lawyers should be running to courts’ to stop coal approvals after landmark ruling, NSW MP says
articles.summary:
High court finding in favour of Hunter Valley community group sets precedent other environmentalists should follow, advocate says

A landmark decision in Australia’s first climate change high…
articles.byline: Donna Lu, Lisa Cox, and Adam Morton

blocks.text: A landmark decision in Australia’s first climate change high court case has been described as a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that exported greenhouse gas emissions “cannot simply be ignored”.

On Wednesday morning, the nation’s highest court ruled that the approval of MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine expansion in NSW’s Hunter Valley was invalid, in a judgment that sets a precedent for fossil fuel projects in the state.

The coal company brought the high court case after a local community group, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg), halted the coalmine expansion on climate grounds in the NSW court of appeal.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burnt overseas. Known as scope 3 emissions, these are not counted in Australia’s domestic tally.

Commenting on the judgment, the deputy Greens leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said: “For too long, big coal and gas companies have tried to pretend that the emissions from their products are someone else’s problem once they leave Australian shores. They’re not.
“When Australian coal is burned overseas, the climate damage doesn’t magically disappear at the port. It comes back to communities here through worsening heat, drought, bushfires and floods.
“This judgment sends a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that the climate impacts of their projects cannot simply be ignored or pushed down the line.”

NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson, formerly a public interest environmental lawyer, also said the high court judgment could lead to “significant legal difficulty” for the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension, which was approved by the IPC a week ago.

In greenlighting the HVO extension – the biggest in the state’s history – the IPC ruled that emissions from the mine would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”, but that their impacts had been outweighed by economic benefits to the region.

For both the HVO and Mount Pleasant coal developments, 98% of the emissions were scope 3 emissions, Higginson said. “HVO’s environmental impact statement didn’t even account for scope 3 emissions at all, and the high court has been crystal clear that consent authorities must ensure emissions are minimised to the greatest extent practicable. It seems clear that the approval of HVO fails this test.
“Lawyers should be running to the courts right now with this judgment in hand, ready to stop coal approvals in their tracks,” she said.

In a joint statement, the Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, and the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, described the decision as a threat to “Australia’s standing as a reliable energy exporter” and said the federal and NSW governments “must act immediately to fix the law”.
after newsletter promotion

“A project extension the Independent Planning Commission approved in 2022, after years of assessment, has been sent back to square one,” they said, arguing that the Minns government should amend NSW’s Environmental Planning and Assessment Act to “make clear that overseas emissions from Australia’s exported resources are not a consideration in project approvals”.
The climate change minister, Chris Bowen, who is in Fiji chairing climate negotiations, said: “The law of the land is law of the land, as interpreted by the high court, and we respect that.

“If others don’t, if others are so biased in their approach that they don’t respect the law of the land, that’s a matter for them. It says a bit about their approach, but that’s about as all I’m going to say because it’s a court case and I’m not in Australia at the moment.”

Murray Watt, the federal environment minister, said on Wednesday afternoon that while he had not had an opportunity to review the judgment in full, “the decision from the high court is in relation to a New South Wales government decision based on New South Wales legislation”.
“It doesn’t automatically transfer to commonwealth decisions or commonwealth legislation,” he told News24.
The NSW government was contacted for comment.

articles.title: Coalition MPs concede immigration pledge not fully costed by independent watchdog
articles.summary: Angus Taylor says opposition ‘worked closely’ with Parliamentary Budget Office but Liberal sources say it has not yet conducted a full analysis of the policy Get our new political email , free app or…

blocks.text: Coalition MPs concede the party’s newly released immigration policy has not been costed in full by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), despite Angus Taylor defending the plan as “budget neutral”.

Taylor, and the deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, have said repeatedly the Coalition “worked closely” with the independent budget watchdog on its plan to reduce net overseas migration to 100,000 for two years.
Announced on Tuesday, the policy would see net overseas migration rates of 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in the fourth.
Business and the university sector have warned the cuts are arbitrary, dangerous for the economy and likely to exacerbate shortages in key sectors, including health and aged care.

Taylor’s office said they planned to have the policy costed before the next federal election, but have used internal analysis and existing costings during the design process. Coalition sources told Guardian Australia the PBO had not conducted a full analysis of the new policy before its release.
PBO officials are not allowed to discuss costings for members of parliament but can choose to clarify references in media reports if they are incorrect or misrepresent PBO work.
The PBO declined to comment on Wednesday.
“We’ve been working closely with the Parliamentary Budget Office on analysis of our initiatives and we are confident that this package is budget neutral,” Taylor said announcing the plan on Tuesday.
He said the Coalition had “done exactly what the government does” and then accused Labor of not releasing modelling.
Labor and One Nation both want to bring down international arrivals, seeking to capitalise on growing anti-migration sentiment and pressure on housing and essential services.
A policy document said the Coalition had worked with the PBO to assess “the impact of the package on the budget”, finding it would generate a small positive return.
Challenged over the release of PBO costings on Wednesday, Taylor told Channel Nine: “We’ve released the outcomes of that budget analysis that we’ve been doing …
after newsletter promotion
“We have released the figures, and we’ve said it’s budget neutral, and we’ve laid that out.”

blocks.caption: Labor announces new visa rules for foreign students bringing family to Australia – video

blocks.text: The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, warned that the Coalition plan would hurt agriculture, aged care and even defence.
“What we see from the Liberal party is actually policy chasing One Nation rather than policy in the national interest,” he said during a visit to Perth.

“Immigration is absolutely central to this. We need to get the numbers right. We do need to manage them down. That’s what our government’s doing, but we need to do it in a way which can maintain our economy and maintain vital sectors like the defence industry here in Western Australia.”
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss, Andrew McKellar, rejected the planned cuts, arguing Australia had a housing supply problem, not an immigration problem.

“When we look at what the Coalition has said, even when we look at what the government and One Nation have said, the problem is each of them are starting from the proposal that they’re targeting a net overseas migration figure. That’s the wrong place to start.”

articles.title: Flydubai attack investigation widens as alleged hijacker’s training in New Zealand scrutinised
articles.summary: Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in Melbourne New Zealand authorities have launched their own…
articles.byline: Eva Corlett in Auckland and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne

blocks.text: New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, 29, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.

Hammami, an Omani national, had allegedly used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air, the United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said. Israeli and other officials in the region suspect he originally planned for such an attack in July, but postponed it.
The New Zealand police assistant commissioner, Michael Johnson, on Tuesday confirmed the man was in the country on a student visa for 175 days, from 30 November 2018 to 23 May 2019.
“Police can confirm the co-pilot was in New Zealand to complete a portion of his flight training for a UK-based company, no longer operating in New Zealand,” Johnson said in a statement
The police are now investigating his time in the country, Johnson said.
New Zealand joins multiple countries scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted alone.

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree, RMIT University in Melbourne confirmed.
On a now deleted social media profile believed to belong to Hammami, the then student appears in a selfie with other teenagers in a shopping centre food court in Melbourne’s CBD.

The UK’s Telegraph reported on a post on a now deleted X account that appears to be linked to Hammami that described his years studying overseas as “the golden years of my religious commitment”, and claimed he became less observant when he returned to Oman.
On Wednesday, Australia’s peak Jewish body, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, called for a thorough investigation of Hammami’s associations in the country.

“We have seen over the years the availability of extremist literature in religious bookstores, the presence of preachers of hate and violence and the capacity for those living in Australia to fall under the sway of recruiters and nefarious street preachers,” the council’s co-chief executive, Alex Ryvchin, said in a statement.
“We have to understand who associated with this [alleged] terrorist, who influenced him and what vestiges of his murderous ideology remain.”
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, who also trained in New Zealand for a time, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.

In a phone call on Saturday with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

articles.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
articles.summary: Some running in November's elections are deciding whether to distance themselves from an unpopular president who still dominates his party.

blocks.text: As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.
"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.
While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.
Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."
There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.

But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.

Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.
When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.
"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."

He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".

In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties.
"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week.

According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most.
"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said.

With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign.
That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right.

"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'"

Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama.
He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.
However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike.

He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are.
"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job."

Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight.
If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him.
"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."

But if Republicans get punished at the ballot box in November, whether they run with the president or away from him, Trump will bear the brunt of the consequences - in the form of a hostile Congress with legislative and oversight powers - for the last two years of his presidency.
Top picture credit: BBC / Getty Images

articles.title: Where is Spain headed after the snap election announcement?
articles.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is taking a gamble by calling an early election in Spain. The housing crisis, migration and the rise of the right-wing populist Vox party are all likely to dominate the…

image.caption: Early on Monday morning, Prime Minister Sanchez announced snap parliamentary electionsImage: LA MONCLOA/AFP

blocks.text: Spain's economic data has been positive recently, but politically, the country has been mired in a prolonged crisis for months.
On Monday, the social democratic Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez responded with a surprise move to break the deadlock: He is calling an early election for November 29.
Why is Sanchez calling an election now?

The sudden announcement followed a dramatic political defeat for the government. On Friday, October 2, Sanchez's emergency measures to tackle the housing crisis failed in parliament. Seven lawmakers from the conservative Catalan separatist party Junts, whose support the government has relied on since 2023, brought the measures down. Sanchez says he is now calling for a "much broader progressive majority."

blocks.caption: Set to profit from the snap election: Vox leader Santiago AbascalImage: Gabriela Sardá Núñez/Europa Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: The defeat came after months of growing instability in the government's parliamentary base. Spain's parliament has not passed a regular budget since 2023.

The recent crisis over mass migration to Ceuta and several corruption scandals involving allegations against the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and people close to Sanchez have piled pressure onto the government.
And then came Maricarmen. The forced eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal last month suddenly turned the housing shortage into the headline political issue.
The fact that his emergency measures were rejected in parliament allows Sanchez to position himself as a defender of tenants. However, it remains to be seen whether that strategy will pay off.
What role is pressure from the street protests playing?

The housing shortage has been at the top of Spaniards' list of concerns for around three years. According to estimates by the Bank of Spain, the country is currently short of around 750,000 homes, and the figure could exceed one million by 2028.

More than half of 18- to 34-year-olds live with their parents or depend on them financially. Property prices have recently been rising three times as fast as wages. In Spain, social housing accounts for just around 1.7 percent of the country's housing stock, putting it at the lower end of the EU scale in comparison with other member states.
Housing crisis triggers snap election in Spain

It is hardly surprising, then, that protest camps sprang up in Madrid and elsewhere in response to the plight of Maricarmen Abascal, and tens of thousands took to the streets across the country. After the government's measures were rejected, the trade unions CCOO and UGT even announced a 24-hour general strike.

These dividing lines, however, do not simply split the government and the opposition. The tenants' movement also views Sanchez's plans as insufficient. The conservative opposition People's Party (PP) and parts of the business community, meanwhile, warn that tighter rent controls could make the problem worse.
Is Sanchez's model of governance coming to an end?

Since the 2023 election, Pedro Sanchez has governed without a majority in parliament. His social democratic PSOE formed a coalition with the left-wing Sumar alliance, but also depended on the support of smaller parties. These included Basque and Catalan regional parties, but above all the Catalan separatists of Junts.

That meant its seven lawmakers were repeatedly able to determine whether government legislation secured a majority or not. Over the course of the parliamentary term, this arrangement became increasingly unstable. In the first half of 2026 alone, the government lost almost one in four votes.

blocks.caption: For three years, the government has failed to get a budget through parliamentImage: Elisabetta Trevisan/Vatican Media/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Evidence of the extent of this political deadlock is the state budget: Spain continues to work with the 2023 budget because the prime minister has been unable to get a new budget through parliament in his entire term. Junts ultimately refused to support Sanchez on housing policy, leaving him without backing on an issue that has been at the top of the political agenda following nationwide protests.
What was the political fallout of the Ceuta crisis?

At the end of July, more than 70,000 people crossed the border from Morocco into Ceuta within a short period of time. Although the government declared the crisis over soon afterward, at least 10,000 migrants were still in the exclave two months later, which has a population of only around 80,000. It was not until last Sunday that police cleared an improvised camp where around 3,000 people had been living.
Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing

The crisis altered Sanchez's previously relatively liberal migration policy. A new draft seen by Reuters proposes accelerated asylum procedures and deportations, as well as tighter rules. Human rights organizations have voiced sharp criticism.
How strong is the opposition?
At first glance, Spain's conservative PP is entering the snap parliamentary election at the end of November as the frontrunner to become the largest parliamentary group.

The real winner of recent months, however, is the right-wing populist Vox party. It is now polling at just over 18%, around six percentage points more than in the 2023 election. A strong Vox turnout could increase PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo's chances of gathering enough seats for a governing majority from parties right of center.

blocks.caption: The man hoping to become Spain's next prime minister: PP leader Alberto Nunez FeijooImage: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Vox leader Santiago Abascal is now confidently setting conditions for cooperation. Priority for Spanish citizens, economic deregulation and a significantly tougher migration policy, including the far-right concept of deporting foreign nationals to their countries of origin.

For his part, Feijoo faces a difficult balancing act. To replace Sanchez, he also needs to win voters from the political center. At the same time, he may need a partner for a governing majority who is steering the campaign significantly further to the right.
Will Spain also be voting on Trump and Europe's political direction?

In international media coverage, Sanchez is repeatedly portrayed as Europe's most prominent critic of Donald Trump. The prime minister rejected the US president's demand for defense spending to rise to 5% of GDP, refused to allow US bases in Spain to be used for the war against Iran and criticized US-Israeli attacks.

As a result, Trump even threatened at one point to cut off trade relations. At the same time, Sanchez explicitly contrasts his more liberal migration policy with Trump's deportation policies and attacks what he calls the "tech oligarchs" from the United States.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez (left) has positioned himself as a strong European voice against Donald TrumpImage: Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sanchez is also one of the most prominent social democratic leaders of a major EU country. If the left were to lose the upcoming Spanish election, the European Council would lose one of its most outspoken voices against Donald Trump . It would also lose a prime minister who has opposed climbing defense spending, defended a more liberal approach to migration and criticized Israel more sharply over the war in Gaza than most of his European counterparts.
This article originally appeared in German.

articles.title: EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars
articles.summary: Mood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese imports EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at…

blocks.text: EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars into Europe.
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday.
Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, where China is high on the agenda.

The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months.

Diplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024 there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars, which were not subject to tariffs.
Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted.

It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries.

On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice.

In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”.

The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”.

Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”.

Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.”
after newsletter promotion

Sources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called “trade bazooka” available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used.
Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement.

Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”.

“Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon didn’t talk about Jesse Baird to friend in lead-up to alleged murders, court hears
articles.summary: NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering his ex and Luke Davies in a Sydney terrace in February 2024 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Despite an alleged…

blocks.text: Despite an alleged obsession with his ex, Beau Lamarre-Condon never spoke about him to a close friend in the three months before allegedly murdering him, a jury has heard.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering his ex-partner Jesse Baird and the man’s new boyfriend Luke Davies in a Sydney terrace in February 2024.

The former senior constable says the two men died in two separate violent struggles with him over his police pistol, and his subsequent efforts to dispose of their bodies were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths.
Much evidence in the NSW supreme court trial’s first three weeks has centred on Lamarre-Condon’s alleged growing obsession with Baird in the year leading up to the killings.
The prosecution alleges the then-police officer became infatuated with Baird after they broke off contact in November 2023, resolving to murder him.
However, Lamarre-Condon’s close friend Nicole Harvell told the court on Wednesday she could not remember any conversation with the ex-officer about Baird after the pair broke up for the final time.
That was despite her being in almost daily contact with the now-31-year-old.

blocks.caption: Evidence and testimony in week two of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s trial – video

blocks.text: Harvell, a police senior constable, recalled trying to contact her friend when she saw media reports that he was under suspicion for the two men’s deaths.
“Fuck Beau, are you ok?” she texted to Lamarre-Condon’s phone.
She never received a reply.
The sworn officer maintained under cross-examination that the accused killer had months earlier told her about enlisting his mother to help him lie to Baird.
Lamarre-Condon posted an Instagram story with a bunch of flowers and the caption: “When he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these.”
after newsletter promotion
But publication was restricted to select friends that did not include Baird.
The photo was designed to imply Baird had sent flowers to the accused, despite the pair not being in a relationship at the time, Harvell said.
When Baird discovered the ruse, Lamarre-Condon spent $160 on a bouquet identical to the photo to lie to him, the officer’s friend said.
Lamarre-Condon then sent a photo to Baird showing his mother with the fresh bouquet.
The bouquet had a handwritten note to imply his mother had been the intended recipient and they were from her partner, who was in Melbourne, the jury heard.
“I recall the accused telling me his mother had written that note,” Harvell said.
The trial continues.

Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones

New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense…

blocks.text: New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed.

Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities.

“The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian.
